item.title: Star Wars: Zero Company maker Bit Reactor is bringing back developers who were furloughed ahead of launch. Read more
item.description:
Star Wars: Zero Company maker Bit Reactor is bringing back developers who were furloughed ahead of launch.
"This week, we started the process of returning more of our team back to work at Bit Reactor, an important step forward in our continued support for Zero Company," studio CEO Greg Foertsch said in an online statement from today. "Having to ask team members to step away after we navigated unexpected business developments outside of our control and so close to launch was an incredibly difficult decision, but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible.
"This team means a tremendous amount to me, and I am incredibly proud of what we have accomplished together," Foertsch continued. "Thank you to our fans for the incredible response to the game and for supporting us along this journey. We look forward to sharing more updates regarding Bit Reactor and Zero Company soon."
Weeks before the acclaimed tactics game came out, the studio reportedly furloughed around 80% of its workforce, which means "most" staff were sent on a leave of absence without pay or benefits. Bit Reactor seemingly ran out of cash to pay its workers, following a legal battle between co-founders Alison Kelly and Foertsch, who has sole ownership of the company.
Bit Reactor doesn't specify how many of its developers have returned to work, though Game File recently reported that more than half of the studio's overall headcount is back on payroll, citing a source familiar with the situation. A fair number of workers are still left in limbo, then.
Star Wars: Zero Company was a big hit right out of the gate, quickly selling over 1m copies and winning over fans by transporting XCOMs best bits to a galaxy far, far away. Here's hoping the rest of the team can come back soon.

item.title: Sony reportedly wants to revive a selection of its long-dormant PlayStation classics with the help of smaller third-party developers, and a new Ape Escape game is apparently up first. Read more
item.description:
Sony reportedly wants to revive a selection of its long-dormant PlayStation classics with the help of smaller third-party developers, and a new Ape Escape game is apparently up first.
The tidbit comes courtesy of The Jeff Gerstmann podcast, where Gerstmann said that a new Ape Escape was on the way from Evening Star, the independent team who made the fan-favorite Sonic Mania before forming their own studio and releasing the surprisingly delightful Penny's Big Breakaway. VGC corroborated the podcast's claims, as well.
"I don't think this game is close to being out or anything like that, but I guess it's been almost a year since we started talking about Ape Escape," Gerstmann said. "Who is making it? That's a good question. My understanding is that it’s an external studio. You know, because people were immediately like, 'Oh, Team Asobi (Astro Bot) is making it.' My understanding is that an external team has been working on that… Evening Star. I heard that they were working on it."
VGC also reported that PlayStation isn't stopping with Ape Escape, either - the console maker is apparently keen to work with other outside developers on some of its legacy IP. It's the same blueprint Sony used for 2025's Everybody's Golf: Hot Shots, which was handled by Bandai Namco.
Ape Escape was a beloved series of 3D platformers during PS1 and PS2 generations, and had players running around levels and catching chaos-causing apes with special gadgets. The last mainline game in the series was 2005's Ape Escape 3, though a lovely playable tribute was also included in Astro Bot.
Speaking of, Astro Bot was a good reminder of just how many classic games PlayStation is sitting on, so there's certainly a lot to choose from. There's already been rumours of a new Killzone game from People Can Fly (Outriders, Gears of War: Judgement), for one. Which comebacks would you like to see? I'm keeping my fingers crossed for Sly Cooper.

item.title: Microsoft has revealed the first batch of games coming to Xbox Game Pass this month, though subscribers only have a week left to try the award-winning Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 before it waves goodbye. Read more
item.description:
October's undisputed headliner is one of last year's hottest games, EA's Battlefield 6. The large-scale shooter broke series records when it dropped, selling over 7m copies in three days and instantly topping Steam's best-seller charts. Post-launch updates and a surprisingly-involved Top Gun collab have kept the game chugging into this year too, despite layoffs at Battlefield Studios back in March.
The other highlights include seven all-new games launching into Game Pass straight away. Time-loop metroidvania Echo Weaver, road trip adventure game Forever Ago, co-op survive-em-up Deep Dish Dungeon, first-person soulslike Valor Mortis, cute photography romp Bluey's Happy Snaps, co-op roguelike Chained Beast, and city-builder (on the back of a space whale) Beyond These Stars slot into the service on the same day as their full launches.
But Game Pass giveth and Game Pass taketh away. This month's group of leavers include the widely-acclaimed and hugely-celebrated RPG, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which debuted on Game Pass early last year. Some personal favorites, like Donut County and Pacific Drive, aren't sticking around either.
For more, check out our full guide to Xbox Game Pass and see every game in the service.
I have one eyebrow tentatively raised for Deep Dish Dungeon's moody, old-school world, if I can fend off the hordes in Gears of War: E-Day for long enough, that is - are you guys interested in any of the newcomers?

item.title: State of Decay studio Undead Labs has spoken out after rebuying its independence and leaving Xbox last month, revealing it has "got to make some changes" to State of Decay 3 because of layoffs it suffered as a result. Read more
item.description:
State of Decay studio Undead Labs has spoken out after rebuying its independence and leaving Xbox last month, revealing it has "got to make some changes" to State of Decay 3 because of layoffs it suffered as a result.
Studio boss Phillip Holt said this during a wide-ranging conversation with The Game Business, in which he detailed the studio's shifting priorities now it has no "boss" to respond to other than its audience, and while explaining why the co-op zombie survival game seems to have been in development for ages.
"We're pretty close to finishing this game," Holt said. "And there's a lot in it. I think folks that saw us at Gamescom can attest to that. I think our alpha players can attest to that. And obviously, with a significant number of people leaving the company, we've got to make some changes. But I don't think we're dramatically addressing scope in that way."
State of Decay 3 currently has a vague release date of "2027", announced this summer, which allows Undead Labs some scheduling wiggle-room. But the game was originally revealed all the way back in 2020, before slipping out of view for a long time, leading people to wonder about what was going on.
"I don't think it's taken that long, actually," Holt remarked, when speaking about the game's long development. "If you measure it from when State of Decay 2 shipped, yeah, we're approaching eight years. If you measure it from our first trailer with the infamous zombie deer, that's also a long time. I got myself in a little bit of trouble by saying we didn't really have a team working on the game at that point, which wasn't entirely true, we had a very small team. We've had a small team on the game since maybe 2020. But development didn't really pick up until 2022 or 2023."
But why did Undead Labs announce the third State of Decay game so early? The answer is eerily prophetic, and it's to do with the spending spree Microsoft was on when it acquired Undead Labs in 2018 - the same spending spree that saw it acquire Ninja Theory, Compulsion Games, and Playground Games (two of which are also no longer a part of Xbox). Holt wanted to announce State of Decay 3 before Undead Labs was "swallowed up or divested" by the rest of a much bigger gaming division, he said.
"I didn't think Microsoft was done being acquisitive," Holt explained, "and I didn't think they'd continue buying small developers - I assumed they'd start buying big things. I was a little worried about getting swallowed up or divested before we had a chance to present to the world what we were working on. So, it was a bit of a marker on the table. I was saying, 'State of Decay 3, we're announcing it, the audience knows it's in development, and here's a trailer to demonstrate our vision.'"
Undead Labs was eventually earmarked for divestiture this summer when Xbox announced its major restructuring. At the time, Undead Labs was said to have "entered terms to join new ownership", but that new-ownership deal - as in the case of Ninja Theory - never actually materialised. "We had a lot of interest," Holt assured The Game Business, but when he heard other studios were doing management buyouts, he submitted one for Undead Labs, "and Microsoft thought that would be a good idea".
Holt wouldn't say how many people were laid off as a result of the studio downsizing to operate independently, "because these are our friends and colleagues and it was a total heartbreak to have to part ways". "I would hate to reduce the impact to those individuals to a number or statistic," he said. But he insisted the studio had "everything we need to ship State of Decay 3", and that its mission was now even clearer.
"Inside of a larger company, you serve multiple objectives and you have directives that you need to achieve," Holt said. "Now it's just: make the best possible game. Of course, inside Xbox, that was also the primary objective. But it's just a cleaner, clearer line of sight to the audience. I don't have a boss. The success or failure of the company is down to whether we create something an audience will support.”
State of Decay 3 will still launch on Game Pass on day one, and Holt praised Xbox's subscription service as being partly responsible for the series' ongoing success, which has apparently seen it reach 25 million players over its lifetime. "I don't know that we'd be in the place we are today if not for the Game Pass audience," he acknowledged. "Even today, we have several thousand people coming through the door every day."

item.title: Call of Duty recently kicked off a week of Modern Warfare 4 DMZ news, which brought us a first look at the "action extraction" mode and some insight into developer Infinity Ward's guiding philosophy. Read more
item.description:
Call of Duty recently kicked off a week of Modern Warfare 4 DMZ news, which brought us a first look at the "action extraction" mode and some insight into developer Infinity Ward's guiding philosophy.
Although more reveals are promised, what's been confirmed so far left one of the biggest questions hanging over DMZ unanswered. Namely, whether the mode is going to offer a PvE-only playlist for those not keen on fighting other players. Dedicated PvE is something that inevitably gets brought up with every new extraction shooter, as we've recently seen with Arc Raiders, Bungie's Marathon, and Escape from Tarkov before that. So, does Modern Warfare 4's DMZ have anything to offer PvE players? Infinity Ward hasn't said, but players picked up on some clues seen in recent trailers.
This all started with episode seven of From the Ward, a behind-the-scenes feature that takes us inside the studio. The focus of that episode was entirely on DMZ and it naturally showed a lot of gameplay. At minute 7:34 into the video, we see the deployment screen with four options. Three of the four are discussed, and have on-screen descriptions - except for Single Squad Mission, which suspiciously has neither.
For players eager to get any confirmation of a PvE-only mode, it was a welcome surprise. The name implies the lobby is limited to a single squad, meaning it's a game players can only join through an invite.
Players took to Reddit and X to ask if the name actually implies what they thought it does, with some tagging the official Call of Duty account directly. While many agree with the basic definition, others believe it's referring to something else.
"Could be a solely PvE mode for DMZ. Would be great if true as I'd rather not have to spend however long getting decent gear just to get wiped by a super," one Reddit user wrote.
Other players, however, think it has to do with DMZ's Lieutenant Hunts, a high-risk encounter type. Defeated Lieutenants drop their Dog Tag, and the player has to extract safely with it for the hunt to count. The counter theory, then, is that Single Squad means only one tag will drop, meaning only a single squad (or player) can extract with it. This is admittedly a weaker explanation, but in the absence of an official description, players are left to come up with their own.
Disrupting that state of affairs was another official trailer, released just one day later. The DMZ Dynamic Ops trailer spotlights one of the four options we referred to earlier. However, when the trailer shows the deployment screen, Single Squad is suspiciously absent.
So what does this mean? It's likely the trailers show different builds of Modern Warfare 4. It's not hard to believe an older build of the game having Single Squad, before it was either removed or pushed back to a post-launch season.
It's also possible Single Squad is an option only available to new players to help with onboarding. The player in the From the Ward video is level 5, compared to level 28 in the most recent trailer. It's not uncommon for multiplayer games to offer low-stress modes to ease newcomers into the experience - rival shooter Battlefield 6 has done it, and many battle royale games, such as Fortnite, limit new players to bot-only matches in their first few levels.
All of that speculation and discourse has once again highlighted the need for a PvE mode. In recent weeks, Infinity Ward did what many thought was unthinkable in adding a silly skin off toggle in Warzone and changing double XP tokens to count down in-match and not in real-time. I could see PvE DMZ being next on that list - even if it's planned for sometime after release.
"Really strange for me why they didn't add PvE from [the] start. Just watch [Escape from] Tarkov with both modes, everybody looks happy with that," wrote another.
DMZ is part of Modern Warfare 4, and is available at its launch on 23rd October for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.description:
Monster Hunter Rise is coming to Android and iOS through Netflix, new store listings have revealed today. The game, which originally launched on Nintendo Switch in 2021 and later came to PC, Xbox and PlayStation - and that I thought was superb, even in its most barebones release state - seemingly got a 'soft launch' today on both Apple and Android storefronts.
The pages note that a Netflix Membership is required in order to download and play the game, but it's important to note that it will be stored and run natively on your mobile device. We've already seen Capcom scale the build up from Switch to PS5 in the past five years, so going the other way and getting the ambitious game running on mobile hardware seems like the logical next step for the publisher. Either way, it's impressive.
The mobile game will have some minor differences to the version you've played elsewhere, including, per the store listing:
I'll be trying this out when it launches properly because I'm curious what touch controls on a full-fat Monster Hunter game feel like. I'm also curious about the timing of this; Capcom is choosing to release a bonafide, mainline Monster Hunter game natively on mobile games just as Tencent's Monster Hunter Outlanders gets ready for launch (it's coming to mobile devices on 29th October). That game is sold as a "fully featured" open-world survival game, replete with the expected gacha mechanics, of course, so it's odd to see both games barging into the fray in the same month.
Just yesterday, Capcom announced that Monster Hunter Rise has officially sold 20 million units worldwide. Is that why the publisher has opted to allow its game to be added to Netflix's game streaming catalogue? What does this mean for the game, and other potential Capcom collaborations, in the future? Phoenix Wright, anyone? For what it's worth, Rise is now on pace with World, which is estimated to have sold 22.4 million units. Last year's upstart, Wilds, is on about 11 million - though Capcom hopes the Switch 2 version and the upcoming Ascendance DLC will shore up those figures somewhat.

item.title: Forza Horizon 6's highly-anticipated release on PlayStation 5 has apparently been delayed to 2027, according to new information. Yes, this is not the first time we've heard that - The Verge's Tom Warren and IGN said as much in late August. Read more
item.description:
Forza Horizon 6's highly-anticipated release on PlayStation 5 has apparently been delayed to 2027, according to new information. Yes, this is not the first time we've heard that - The Verge's Tom Warren and IGN said as much in late August.
Forza Horizon 6 studio Playground Games countered those claims days later, however, saying the open-world driving game has not been pushed back, while opening wishlisting for it on the PlayStation Store.
Now, Dealabs' reliable leaker billbil-kun has added their voice to the noise, going further by revealing a specific, 26th January release date. They also speculated that an official announcement is coming this week alongside the opening of pre-orders.
"We've done our own investigation, and our research has paid off. Yes, we've managed to obtain the exact release date of Forza Horizon 6 on PS5," wrote French insider billbil-kun (via machine translation).
According to billbil-kun, the game is priced £59.99 in the UK and €69.99 in the rest of Europe. A physical version - with a disc - will also be available at retail. Incidentally, billbil-kun wasn't able to verify whether a Premium Edition is being offered on PS5.
On PC and Xbox, the Premium Edition includes an expansion pass, car pass and various other in-game bonuses. If purchased ahead of launch, the Premium Edition also grants up to four days of early access. It's possible Xbox is planning to release a digital-only Premium Edition on PS5, which wouldn't be visible to billbil-kun's typically retail-based sources.
Just yesterday, Playground Games issued a statement on X apologising for a general lack of communication about Forza Horizon 6 and assuring players it was listening to feedback. The developer also promised to look into changing the way it communicates with players going forward.
Of course, it's always possible the decision to delay Horizon 6 to January was made after Playground announced it was on track for a 2026 release, even though it's been almost exactly one month since.
Forza Horizon 6 has been one of the best-selling games this year so far. It continues to attract players each week, and is estimated to be the highest-grossing new release on Steam in 2026 so far. In the Eurogamer Forza Horizon 6 review, Dom Peppiatt said the game has reached the zenith of the Horizon off-shoot spirit despite not really reinventing the wheel.

item.title: Aion 2 has arrived, and there's a lot to like if you've got a hankering for a new MMO: meaty combat, challenging boss encounters, a seemingly endless grind for completionists, and, yes, it's free to play. However, one of my very favourite things about it is the character creator. Read more
item.description:
Aion 2 has arrived, and there's a lot to like if you've got a hankering for a new MMO: meaty combat, challenging boss encounters, a seemingly endless grind for completionists, and, yes, it's free to play. However, one of my very favourite things about it is the character creator.
Like many South Korean MMOs, much love has been poured into Aion 2's character creator. It comes with countless adjustable settings, allowing players to tweak each facial feature to the minutest detail, as well as some truly adventurous facial markings and hair styles. I tend to start every new MMO with a few spins of the character randomiser; fishing for inspiration with each new roll. And with Aion 2, I struck gold.
Suddenly, there he was: a tiny man with bright red eyes and green hair, his gut looming over stumpy legs; a different sort of hero. I rolled up my sleeves and started to finesse: I made his jawline flat and angular, his mouth blobfish wide. I changed his hair to the most irregular option I could find, and giggled at my ridiculous, magnificent creation.
The best video game character creators, I reckon, let you make both beauty and beast. Some people - the vast majority, perhaps - get pleasure making cool protagonists, handsome and strong in a way that plays into the classic hero fantasy. That's okay, obviously. But the freedom to get a bit weird with it offers a different kind of joy.
Aion 2's story is fine. It's an unremarkable tale of grave threats and devilish forces out to do bad things to good people. But drop in a character alien to this very serious world - in both looks and vibe - and the disconnect creates friction. Story cinematics might lose their gravitas when everyone else is looming over my silly looking guy, but I get a real kick out of his jarring presence, and he brightens every step of an otherwise straight-faced adventure.
Take pets, for example. Much of Aion 2's customisation and player power comes from these collectibles. They're found by killing enemies, and their models vary wildly - some monstrous, some not. You can ride pets as mounts, increasing ground movement, and I can't get enough of the Krall Laborer - an orcish humanoid with a broad build and permanent scowl. It pairs perfectly with my small fella who rides on its shoulder, me giggling as we rugby run through the world.
I've got such a kick out of my silly goober over the last week that I've spent real-world money on premium cosmetics to make him stand out even more in this fantastical world. I bought the loose-fit streetwear outfit for just over £20, giving him a chain, a bum bag, and a pink baseball cap. Maybe that makes me the silly goober, but it was worth every penny. I don't care.
And it turns out Aion 2 offers some surprisingly practical perks for atypical heroes like my portly pal. For one, this is a fast-paced action MMO with many movement features, obstacle-vaulting among them. And as a character of smaller stature, my green-haired guy flips over logs and other low barriers with pleasing dexterity.
So, here's to the games like Aion 2 - games with the kind of character creators that aren't afraid to let you go wild, and aren't afraid to let you bring some of your own silly personality into the adventure. It's a pretty good MMO too, even if you don't want to play as a miniscule fiery eyed plonker.

item.title: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly told the company that Xbox has "started to return to growth" following wide-ranging restructuring that has reorganised the gaming division and resulted in more than 1,800 job losses. Read more
item.description:
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly told the company that Xbox has "started to return to growth" following wide-ranging restructuring that has reorganised the gaming division and resulted in more than 1,800 job losses.
"We're making the right decisions to reinvest in the business," Sharma reportedly said during an Xbox 'town hall' meeting, according to a transcript seen by Windows Central. "After an all-time low, we've started to return to growth, more than two to three times what we were, and we expect that continue."
Sharma specifically named the games Gears of War: E-Day, Minecraft Dungeons 2 and World of Warcraft: Forever - all recent releases - as having had "strong" starts and contributing to this.
Sharma reportedly also said Xbox had seen a decline in hours played, player numbers and revenue at the start of the year. The situation has seemingly improved, with the decline in hours played apparently now stabilised.
On Game Pass, Sharma said Xbox's previous strategy had sent the service's profitability "into freefall". She's likely referring to Xbox's decision to include Call of Duty titles in Game Pass on day one, which later pushed the company to raise Game Pass prices in 2025, before cutting prices in 2026 at the cost of losing day-one Call of Duty.
"Why do we exist?" Sharma reportedly asked. "We exist to be where the world plays, we will know when we have a billion daily active people, and we have a right to win because we're now focused on our fans and franchises."
As part of the same town hall meeting, Sharma touched on Xbox's broader plans with Project Helix, its next-generation console. The executive reaffirmed earlier remarks for Helix to be "a family of devices", and teased another foray into the handheld market - beyond the ROG Ally X - by referencing that people want to game "on the go".
Xbox has had a turbulent year since Sharma took over as CEO in February. Shortly after her appointment, she announced a major shake-up and restructuring plan for the gaming division that would encompass wide-ranging layoffs, studio divestitures, a focus on its biggest franchises and the introduction of new business models for both Xbox hardware and services. That restructuring work is not expected to be completed until next summer.

item.title: Microsoft has reportedly reiterated its plan to have multiple Xboxes - of some description - for the next and 10th generation of consoles. The suggestion being that there's a main console accompanied by some kind of portable, on-the-go games machine. Read more
item.description:
Microsoft has reportedly reiterated its plan to have multiple Xboxes - of some description - for the next and 10th generation of consoles. The suggestion being that there's a main console accompanied by some kind of portable, on-the-go games machine.
The suggestion comes from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, who was talking yesterday at a company 'town hall' meeting that Windows Central was reportedly sent a transcript of. "We are moving to a family of devices for Gen-10," Sharma is reported as saying. "There is not one device that fits all.
"We will certainly have a great console first," Sharma added, "but we also know that many players will be on the go. There are some things that we are the best in the world to manufacture, and there are other things that we will partner on. So, we will be sharing more about that as our plans develop. The operating system is starting to look really good. We're very excited about this."
This is not the first time Microsoft has talked about next-generation plans, nor about its desire for Project Helix - as the next-generation Xbox hardware is codenamed - to be a "family" of devices. Sharma said almost the same thing to the BBC recently, stating: "We've been hard at work on a great next generation and a great family of devices for Helix, and we'll share more soon."
Sharma isn't reported as saying anything more about Helix during the Xbox town hall meeting, but she has previously said "Project Helix will lead in performance and play your Xbox and PC games", suggesting a kind of hybrid nature. Whether or not it will have a disc-drive is another burning question as yet unanswered.
Of course, it's not a radical departure at all that Microsoft would want a "family" of Xbox devices. Indeed, it has already used this approach this generation, with Xbox Series S being a more entry-level accompaniment to Xbox Series X, and the Asus ROG Ally X handheld - a partnership with Asus (partnerships being something Sharma referenced in the alleged town hall speech) - providing an Xbox experience on the go. Key to this approach is Xbox's Play Anywhere cross-buy initiative, which lets you buy a game on one platform and play it on others.
A bigger question surrounding Microsoft's next-generation plans relates to the ongoing memory component crisis, which has driven computer hardware prices up enormously, resulting in unprecedented price rises for consoles this generation - and it's an AI-driven shortage that shows no signs of abating or slowing down. Sharma has talked about exploring "radically different business models" in order that people can afford whatever Xbox makes and puts out.

item.description:
Xbox has denied reports suggesting it obtained exclusive game-streaming rights for Grand Theft Auto 6. The initial suggestion came from a report on The Verge, which cited an all-hands meeting in which CEO Asha Sharma allegedly told staff that Xbox plans to do something "no other platform holder is doing" around GTA 6.
The report inferred that Xbox had acquired exclusive game streaming rights for GTA 6, which would allow anyone using Xbox's Cloud Gaming service to stream GTA 6 on any supported platform - including on PC where the game won't natively be available.
Shortly after the report was published, however, Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball took to X to quash the suggestion and said Xbox won't be streaming GTA 6 exclusively, nor will the game be available that way on PC. "While the excitement for GTA 6 and Xbox is great to see," Ball said, "it has also led to some misreporting. We are looking forward to launching GTA 6 on Xbox November 19, though the game will not be streaming exclusively or to PC."
Xbox's cloud streaming service has changed dramatically in recent months. Following Sharma's appointment as CEO, the company has capped the number of Cloud Gaming play-hours available to Game Pass members. After years of no limits, Game Pass users are now limited to just 15 hours per month at the highest tier, Ultimate, which is reportedly a tipping-point where the streaming service stops being profitable for Microsoft.
In November, perhaps timed around the launch of GTA 6, Xbox is also launching Xbox Cloud Gaming as a standalone service that anyone can use without the need for a Game Pass membership. This paid model allows users to buy chunks of playtime hours to stream games they own to supported devices.
Xbox is also exploring different business models around game streaming. The company is already testing an ad-supported, free tier of Cloud Gaming with Xbox Insiders, and a November launch for that tier would make sense.
Beyond the Xbox portion of the report, Rockstar has not announced any GTA 6 streaming deals with any provider, though that could change as we get closer to the game's 19th November release date.

item.title: Of all the games I thought I'd see converted to virtual reality, the Diablo games weren't among them, for some reason. But one industrious modder has set about changing that, converting probably the most well-liked Diablo game, Diablo 2. Read more
item.description:
Of all the games I thought I'd see converted to virtual reality, the Diablo games weren't among them, for some reason. But one industrious modder has set about changing that, converting probably the most well-liked Diablo game, Diablo 2.
Footage of the Diablo 2 VR mod was shared on Reddit and it shows the game being played in first-person, as the Sorceress explores the dingy starting area fields of the game, fireballing zombies and other enemies that are shambling nearby. It seems to work pretty well, with the player's left forearm showing the character's health and mana pools, and toolbar, and the inventory on their belt and map in their hand.
The Diablo 2 VR mod is made by Sergious - Reddit username Fantastic-Author2736 - and the mod files are made available on Github, should you wish to try it. Sergious made the mod with FlatVR and BodyWalk, but you don't need BodyWalk, apparently, to play it.
It's strikingly atmospheric seeing Diablo's world this way, through the character's eyes. The world is usually so far below you, as you look over it like a god from above, from an isometric vantage point. Not for the first time, it's made me wonder what Diablo would be like played from a much closer, over-the-shoulder camera angle, or even a first-person one. I'd half-expected Diablo 5 - recently announced at BlizzCon - to go this way, though it doesn't appear to be.
Meanwhile, in VR land, Valve recently released its much-awaited new Steam Frame headset, which we've reviewed on Eurogamer and we really liked. The drawback, as ever, is cost, with the base version priced £889. But if you can afford it, it offers an impressive and comfortable wireless VR experience, and a way to play non-VR games through a kind of hybrid experience. Perhaps you can play the other Diablo games this way, while Sergious finishes their Diablo 2 VR mod. Chop chop!

item.title: Sega has invited chaos upon itself by launching an official Sonic the Hedgehog Discord channel. Unsurprisingly, it's proven immediately popular, and strictly locked down. There is no fan art channel as of writing. Read more
item.description:
Sega has invited chaos upon itself by launching an official Sonic the Hedgehog Discord channel. Unsurprisingly, it's proven immediately popular, and strictly locked down. There is no fan art channel as of writing.
The announcement, made on official Sega social media accounts, reads as follows: "Looking for a place to chill and chat all things Sonic the Hedgehog? Maybe find people to race in Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds? We are excited to welcome you to the official Sonic Discord server!"
This post, made on X late last night, invited hordes of Sonic fans into the hub all at once, where there are various channels for discussion of Sonic games, movies, and comics. There's even an off-topic channel, which seems potentially unwise, and when Eurogamer explored the Discord server today, strict moderation features were in place.
For example, the server is currently on slow mode, meaning the quantity of posts made in each channel has been drastically reduced. There are also chat limitations in place, preventing newcomers to the server from posting at all unless they use a Discord Nitro boost (a paid service). A plea to "keep it family friendly" is present on the rules page as well.
The moderators posted a launch day Q&A, establishing some additional ground rules for the influx of Sonic fans. It claims over 50,000 people hopped into the server within around six hours, and made it clear a fan-art channel would eventually be coming down the line. It also confirms that posting images has been disabled by default, and an "aggressive" auto filter is removing messages written in all-caps.
Even with these strict rules and harsh moderation practice, cheeky messages have found a way to be sprinkled throughout the chat channels.
However, for the most part, the current state of the Discord server is stable. For the most part, people are spamming the same Discord sticker showing the Sonic mascot running towards the screen. Which, relative to other gifs that could be posted, is harmless fun.
Hopefully, this will be a home for discussion on upcoming Sonic games. Sega was recently hiring for key roles across a variety of teams, indicating Sega could be working on fresh Sonic games, though nothing has been announced as of writing. Sonic Racing: Crossworlds was the latest release and has proved fairly successful, speeding past 1m sales in short order.
How long the Sonic discord will exist, and how long the moderators will last, remains the two big questions. Eurogamer wishes these moderators all the best in the coming weeks.

item.description:
Earlier this week, Blizzard released a new trailer for an upcoming event in Overwatch. Called 'Defiled Anthem', the event features skins and cosmetics for Shion, D.Mon, Kiriko, Reaper, and Emre, with the highlight of the whole activation culminating in a transforming 'Evolution' skin that changes sound effects and visual effects as the match goes on. The only catch? These new skins and cosmetics are China-specific and have not been announced for the rest of the world. This has happened in the past with a Naraka: Bladepoint crossover, as well as exclusive skins for Pharah and Mercy.
Player sentiment, as you can imagine, has been negative: take a look at any Overwatch-focused subreddit or social media account, and you'll see the same complaints cropping up. But why does this happen? Why does Blizzard put out these skins in one region when it knows fans in another are going to complain?
Earlier this year, in an interview with IGN, Blizzard’s head of development for live games, Walter Kong, explained that the addition of Chinese-only skins is largely because of the studio's relationship with Chinese publisher Netease, which handles the promotion and management of the game in the region.
"I think NetEase has the responsibility of publishing our game in China, and part of their approach is to do things that are specific to that market," Kong explained. "And the approach that we want to take is to make sure that our game makes players feel cared for, no matter the market. And I think we fell short of the mark with this current event, but it does mean that as we look forward to future events and activations, we have a very specific view that 'Is this just the right way to run the event?' and from the perspective of holistically, 'How do things balance out?'"
I wouldnt be so mad about China exclusive stuff if it wouldnt constantly be the best skins, emotes and intros in the gameThat Shion skin is better than any Mythic or Ultra skin we have… pic.twitter.com/BYCA5xTjjx
There's a pervasive feeling amongst international players of Overwatch that Chinese fans are 'treated better' than they perhaps are. In the past, players in the region would get free skins that were locked behind battle passes or needing buying in non-Chinese markets. In the past few days, these negative feelings have surfaced again; Reddit threads ask "what's the deal with [Overwatch] China?" whilst players on the dedicated Blizzard forums make accusations about 2023's Japanese character, Shion, being "supposedly claimed by NetEase".
"The problem isn’t about players receiving exclusive content," suggested one person on the Blizzard forums. "It's about Blizzard blatantly throwing in our faces that they're prioritising one region over others. It’s not about the content itself, but the Overwatch devs/designers/staff are preoccupied with only paying attention to China as if it were the only relevant player base. [...] Blizzard owns the Overwatch IP; these changes to exclusive content certainly have Blizzard's full approval."
Despite how Western players complain about their treatment compared to Chinese players, the game isn't without criticisms in that region either. The gacha system in Chinese Overwatch is different to the one the rest of the world uses, and it's managed by NetEase. It is more expensive, and has a 'pity cap' (a mechanic that delivers items to you once you've spent a certain amount) that performs differently to the US or Europe, which is seen as more punishing by local players.
her best highlight intro being china exclusive like ok. what ever. i dont even care anymore. pic.twitter.com/15Jmf1EHgw
Per one dedicated mathematician, you need to spend approximately 1,080 Yuan - $162/£123 - to ensure you pull the sought-after 'Evolution' skin for Shion in this event. Thanks to its 0.02 percent rarity, you require something like 80 to 90 gacha 'pulls' to exhaust the pool of available items before acquiring the cosmetic. That cost, as it happens, is exactly what one unlucky player spent trying to acquire Jetpack Cat's 'Evolution' skin back in August. The upside? Chinese players can resell skins; and from what I can see right now, the Shinon 'Evolution' skin seems to be selling for about 670 Yuan, or $100/£75.

item.description:
The unannounced but consistently leaked Xbox Elite Series 3 controller has, well, leaked again. Details ranging from analogue stick technology to rumble motors and more were dug up from the backend of Xbox's own Design Lab website that lets customers create and order custom controller designs.
The datamined Xbox Elite Series 3 details ended up on Reddit and revealed a number of promising controller additions. For starters, the listing seems to confirm the controller will have Hall Effect and TMR sticks. Unlike traditional analogue sticks, Hall Effect or Tunnel Magnetoresistance (TMR) sticks rely on magnets rather than a physical connection, which eliminates physical problems like wear and stick drift. The wording makes it sound like customers will be able to choose between the two, though it's not clear what the default version is going to be.
There's also a reference to "advanced haptics" for the Elite Series 3 controller, which appears to mirror some of the features of the PlayStation 5's DualSense controller. That plus the return of impulse triggers, which feature their own haptics and multi-stage presses.
Elsewhere in the leak, there's a reference to a dedicated "audio scroll wheel", which some of the earlier leaks have shown. Faceplates can also be customised and replaced, and the controller seemingly offers multiple d-pad choices
Based on the leaked information, it appears Xbox plans to sell two main versions of the Elite Series 3, one dubbed Base and the other Complete. Both versions offer the option of the haptics motor, incidentally, making for a total of four products.
The Elite is Xbox's premium line of controllers, designed for core gamers and competitive players. The most recent iteration, Elite Series 2 Core, debuted in 2022 for £115 / $130, three years after the main, more expensive and feature-rich version at £160 / $180. Given the leak's origin, and how detailed it appears to be, we're likely closer than ever to an official announcement and potential release date.
Meanwhile, of course, Xbox is undergoing seismic changes overseen by newish leader Asha Sharma, which has led to major bouts of layoffs. The most recent of these waves occurred at the end of September, and resulted in 268 layoffs, the migration of the Halo franchise to Activision, and the apparent closure of British studio Ninja Theory.

item.description:
This feels like the kind of admission that's liable to make Miyamoto cross me off his Christmas card list, but my favourite game in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort was the one that required absolutely no energetic prancing at all. A desk yes, which might be a problem in some living rooms, but gleeful flailing, no. Skateboarding is, however, just one of a bunch of activities where Nintendo's exercise-adjacent sports series allows for a more exploratory turn, and, after an hour playing at Gamescom, it's left me excited for more.
I might be getting a bit ahead of myself, though. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort (which, somewhat confusingly, is exclusive to Switch 2) includes a total of 12 motion-controlled events, six of them returning from 2022's Nintendo Switch Sports, six of them new. Or at least returning after a much longer absence, some having previously appeared back in 2009's Wii Sports Resort. Yes, I get the names confused too. Together, then, there's archery, basketball, bowling, boxing, golf, power cruising, prop plane, skateboarding, table tennis, tennis, thumb wrestling, and volleyball. And while my Gamescom hands-on time was far from exhaustive, it was split fairly evenly between traditional events and some of Wuhu Island's more exploratory free-form thrills.
Table tennis, for instance, fell into the former camp, playing a lot like Nintendo's much-loved take on tennis - just transposed to a little table. So if you know Wii Tennis and its successors, you know what to expect here. Switch 2's Joy-Cons do a fine job of translating your requisite paddle whips and wrist flicks onto the screen - which, admittedly, doesn't do you any favours if your table tennis prowess is as cack-handed as mine - but it's a fun time; a more contained counterpoint to tennis' energetic flailing.
Thumb wrestling, meanwhile, is built around even more localised movement, victory requiring little more than determination and an aggressively opposable thumb. It's a hoot too; a rapidfire kind of thrill that quickly descends into a game of sneaky feints, where you grip the Joy-Con vertically in your fist, twist to move your on-screen hand, then press the R button to lower your thumb. The goal, essentially, is to goad your opponent into dropping their thumb first so you can catch it with your own then pin it down as they attempt to wiggle free before the timer hits zero. Failure to do so constitutes a win for you, but escape means the round continues, each successive capture demanding increased waggle to break free. It makes for a swift bit of ridiculousness, yet the slyly strategic mind games involved nudges it beyond mere frivolity.
Archery, too, makes for a strong showing. Here, two Joy-Cons are required per player, but there's the option to take turns if you don't have enough controllers. It's played (in the kind of intuitive verisimilitude reflected across the rest of the package) by adopting a familiar archer's stance: one Joy-Con held out front, the second slightly behind. Joy-Con one acts as your bow, which you move to adjust your aim, and the second is your string, dictating the strength of your arrow as you draw it back - accounting for movement, wind, and height as you go. And there's enough nuance in the set-up, across all the mini-games in fact, that it feels like there's genuine space for skill, which will hopefully help them sustain their appeal.
For this particular showing, I was launching arrows under archery's Special rules, which see players attempting to score points by hitting their designated colour on the target. Hit someone else's though, and the points go to the competition. And while Nintendo's guided tour of Switch Sports Resort didn't leave an enormous amount of time to absorb the finer points of each event, I get the sense most activities feature a variety of different rules and modes. During boxing, for instance, we got a peek at Island Crown mode, providing 20 ranked opponents for solo players to tackle without needing to go online.
It's all good stuff, enhanced by the series' slick presentation. But as much as I enjoyed Switch Sports Resort's more focused matches, it was the freeform interludes that really had me yearning for more. Nintendo whizzed us through three distincts Free Play sports at Gamescom: prop plane, power boating, and, yes, skateboarding; each showing off Wuhu Island - the charming tropical retreat that's been popping up in everything from Mario Kart to Smash Bros. since its original Wii Fit debut - from a different perspective.
It's here Switch Sports Resort flexes its open-world muscles, giving players a time limit in which to accrue the most points as they fly/skate/sail free. Prop plane requires you to hold the Joy-Con like a paper aeroplane, tilting and turning it to glide serenely through the air; angling into hoops, skimming over undulating water, or daredevil-dodging between island landmarks, with little points-of-interest icons given you a bit of tour guide spiel. Freeform power boating, meanwhile, sees you grasping the Joy-Con like handle bars and contorting your body, somewhat unnaturally, to steer up ramps and over more tumultuous waves.
Which brings me to my favourite: skateboarding. Here, you'll need a table to use the Joy-Con in mouse mode. Its flat edge resting on the table's surface, you pull the controller toward you - mirroring a virtual foot pulling back - finding the right rhythm to gather skateboarding speed as you explore Wuhu Island's roadways and exotic corners. But there's more: a quick upward flick does a little leap, onto grind rails perhaps so you can do additional tricks as you go. It's oddly hypnotic, the perfect marriage of motion and on-screen movement, and like all these Free Play detours, strikes a wonderful balance between leisurely exploration and competitive points acquisition - to the point I was genuinely eager for more.
Switch Sports Resort is looking promising then, and suggests Switch 2 could have another family favourite hit to its name as it star-jumps into the festive season - especially if there's enough variety across its 12 events to ensure some proper sticking power. Will any of those other events manage to drag me away from the mesmerising thrills of freeform skateboarding? Nintendo Switch Sports Resort arrives in just a few weeks, so I guess we'll find out soon.

item.title: As a first-party Xbox title, Gears of War: E-Day is under pressure to look good and run well on Xbox consoles. This is especially challenging to do on Series S, due to the console's limited computing power compared to Series X. But developer The Coalition has discovered a clever way of circumventing the Series S' limited memory pool. Read more
item.description:
As a first-party Xbox title, Gears of War: E-Day is under pressure to look good and run well on Xbox consoles. This is especially challenging to do on Series S, due to the console's limited computing power compared to Series X. But developer The Coalition has discovered a clever way of circumventing the Series S' limited memory pool.
Gears of War: E-Day has densely-detailed environments that require a lot of system memory (RAM), which is a struggle for Xbox Series S' 10GB of GDDR6 RAM. The Coalition's solution was to offload some of that data onto the console's ultra-fast NVMe SSD storage drive. Digital Foundry reported on the tech behind it, which was co-developed by Xbox's Advanced Technology Group.
For some context, NVMe SSD drives are made up of RAM modules of their own, so they can act as additional RAM when needed. As fast as they are, however, NVMe drives aren't quite as fast as proper RAM, so The Coalition essentially used the NVMe as a second tier of RAM to help the game's engine stream assets more smoothly. The game then swaps what's needed in the present moment to RAM, and then sends it back to the NVMe when it's not actively being used.
"The benefit is that, in exchange for a couple of gigabytes of storage on the SSD, you can gain about a gigabyte of usable system memory," Digital Foundry's report explained. And, the system is smart enough to cherry-pick chunks of data that won't be heavily impacted by being moved to the slower memory. The system uses "advanced heuristics" to decide which data to move to the NVMe, by analysing access patterns. "Frequently used data stays in RAM, and anything idle can move to the SSD," the report added.
Whether future Xbox games could use similar technology to increase performance on Xbox Series S is of course the big question, especially as large-world games GTA 6 and Fable approach. But though the execution may be unique to Gears of War: E-Day, the idea of swapping data between slow and fast memory isn't entirely new: Mac devices, for instance, are especially good at doing this. Yet as the current console generation ages, clever solutions will be needed to keep up with demands of triple-A games, especially as this generation may last longer than initially intended thanks to ongoing memory shortages.
Incidentally, The Coalition also invested in other engine upgrades throughout E-Day development, such as improving the technology behind gore and dismemberment, because "we had this feeling fans were getting a bit desensitised to the violence in Gears".
It's a potentially important development for Xbox, but it comes at a time when Xbox is in no small amount of disarray as wide-ranging - and ongoing - restructuring rocks Microsoft's gaming division. Staff at The Coalition fear they could be laid off next, following the release of Gears of War: E-Day.

item.title: CD Projekt Red has let The Witcher 3 community know its work isn't done patching the newly-released Remastered edition of the game. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has let The Witcher 3 community know its work isn't done patching the newly-released Remastered edition of the game.
In a post on X, CDPR specified a few areas of the game that are still being looked at. These include "further performance improvements, particularly on PS5", "further visual adjustments", and "voiceover audio fixes on consoles". "We're aiming to address many of these in the next update," CDPR said. "We're also investigating other reported issues, so please keep sharing your reports through [this link]."
CDPR said it's also "working on bringing more mods across all platforms" together with mod.io; cross-platform mod support was added in the Remastered edition of the game. I haven't tested this feature yet but I'm intrigued to see what's available there.
"Please bring back the next-gen version to PS5," read another. "Don't delete for preservation the next-gen version to the people that already owned [it]. For some of us, we prefer the next-gen version. Bring us the option back." You can, incidentally, roll back the game-version on PC without much trouble, but on console, the option isn't there.
The Remastered overhaul of The Witcher 3 significantly updates the game, redrawing textures and environments as well as updating animations and skills in the game. It's a huge undertaking - effectively a 3.0 release - and given that it arrives 11 years into the game's life, and for free, it's an extraordinarily generous thing for CDPR to do. However, it also raises minimum system requirements for the game in the process, putting more strain on older machines.
It's an effort to modernise the by-now legendary RPG ahead of a third and unprecedented expansion - for a single-player game so far from release - arriving next year, called Songs of the Past. And so far, the Remastered edition has not only brought players back in droves, but reinvigorated sales of the game as well.

item.description:
Supermassive Games - the developer behind games such as Directive 8020 and the original Until Dawn - seems to have lost over 70 staff today as part of widespread layoffs at the company.
Supermassive Games previously announced these were coming in August. In a statement posted to social media, the developer wrote: "We have made the difficult decision to begin a redundancy consultation process, which we anticipate will result in the loss of up to 75 of our colleagues. This is a necessary step to ensure the sustainability of our company."
It seems that this layoff process has concluded as of this week, as now-former IT and facilities director Frank Tindle announced his departure on LinkedIn with a fond farewell to other Supermassive staff in the same position as him.
"More than 70 brilliant people are leaving Supermassive: developers, artists, producers, QA, operations and more. Any studio would be lucky to have them. If you're hiring, DM me and I'll make the introduction."
This isn't the first time Supermassive has suffered job cuts in recent memory. Back in July 2025, the studio announced up to 36 employees would be laid off, claiming these cuts would allow them to "adapt our team structure to better align with recent industry changes". This resulted in the delay of Directive 8020, a game that would go on to release this May.
That game proved divisive, with the studio's first dive into sci-fi horror tearing many between a stellar cast of characters and grating stealth gameplay. Still, the studio continues to release unique narrative titles for an audience of passionate fans. Here's hoping the hard times are over for Supermassive, and those impacted by these recent layoffs land on their feet.

item.description:
Who doesn't love a good top-down ARPG; a solid dungeon-crawler with visceral action and real punchy combat that sticks in your teeth like toffee? Aside from Diablo and Path of Exile, there aren't as many out there as I'd like. But Tarae: The Unbound, from South Korean studio Boundary and publisher Krafton, might help change that. I had a chance to get my hands on an early version during this year's Gamescom, and while it's far from finished, what I played of it showed real promise.
Tarae is an isometric action game rooted deeply in Buddhist mythology, and while its demo might be relatively short, it's immediately clear Boundary understands the most important quality of ARPGs: making combat feel good. That starts with a choice between three distinct classes, and, in the demo, I pick the Samurai; a melee-focused fighter who's all about getting up close and wreaking havoc.
You've a dodge roll, a limited stamina bar, and a few healing potions to see you through the dangerous world ahead. And each swing of your sword comes with satisfyingly hefty audio-visual feedback. But it's more than simple slicing and dicing, and includes an intriguing set of abilities that elevates the experience.
Two in the demo stood out to me as especially delightful. The first is a charging slash that shows Boundary understands the importance of weight in games like this. There's nothing worse than floatiness - letting loose a massive blow only for it to flutter from your hands - but Tarae's animators, visual effects artists, and audio engineers are all working in unison here to get the feeling absolutely right. And as I throw myself against foes, blood leaping from them with every charging slash, it's joyous.
Movement - the ability to shift quickly across the battlefield - is another key ARPG element Tarae nails. And that ties into something else I love: its throwable dagger. On its own, it's an unremarkable projectile, but it has additional utility. Once thrown, you can teleport to its resting spot at the press of a button. Doing so causes an eruption around your character, which, when correctly timed, deals damage to all those around you.
All of these abilities can be modified by a wide selection of subskills. But while everything was unlocked for the demo, I only really had a chance to mess around with them briefly. What I saw appeared to be percentile alterations and minor amendments - perhaps not hugely impactful, but as a focus for the finer points of buildcrafting, the extent of options was enticing.
As for the enemies you use these abilities on, the ones I faced could be split into two broad categories. The first are your standard goons; hordes of smaller foes that rush up to slap you or throw projectiles from a distance. These weren't especially challenging, but a careless attention slip could still occasionally leave me grasping for healing potions or spamming the dodge button.
Far more interesting were the two bosses I fought. Despite apparently being the earliest bosses in-game, I was struck by the number of moves they threw at me. The first, a giant toad demon of sorts, served as a bit of a warm-up. It rolled on its side, dashing any hope of a safe spot to strike, while its leaps forced a well-timed dodge to prevent a hefty chunk of damage. Even so, it didn't put up much of a fight and I very much enjoyed unleashing my move set into it.
In contrast, the follow-up fight against a sorcerer was genuinely challenging. A deluge of incoming blows required fairly precise positioning, something that hadn't been required in earlier fights. It also entered a phase of endless invulnerability strikes which persisted until I stood inside a lit space within the arena. Add in a substantial health bar, and I just couldn't quite beat it before the demo's time-limit ended, prompting a disappointed wail from everyone in the room, including me.
Based on my relatively brief hands-on time, Tarae: The Unbound has a solid ARPG foundation. But these sorts of games don't tend to reveal their true greatness until their later hours - when you can delve into the customisation of your character's abilities, discovering a playstyle that suits you best. Likewise, I've only seen glimpses of Tarae's Eastern mythology aesthetic, and I'm eager to see what else it does with its rich setting. Even so, I've a sense this might be one for genre enthusiasts to watch.
This preview is based on a preview at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. Krafton provided flights and accommodation.

item.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 studio Infinity Ward is betting big on DMZ - the game's extraction shooter mode - becoming another major pillar of the series. In a wide-ranging blog post and developer diary, we learn more about the studio's goals, and how the upcoming DMZ builds on 2022's Modern Warfare 2 DMZ beta. Read more
item.description:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 studio Infinity Ward is betting big on DMZ - the game's extraction shooter mode - becoming another major pillar of the series. In a wide-ranging blog post and developer diary, we learn more about the studio's goals, and how the upcoming DMZ builds on 2022's Modern Warfare 2 DMZ beta.
Infinity Ward hopes the new DMZ mode will be an important addition to the genre, referring to the mode several times as the "action extraction shooter", emphasising the mode's focus on combat and engagement over menu navigation and looting - two things synonymous with other extraction shooters. Those elements do exist in DMZ, but from what the developer showed of it, the UI is designed to allow for speedy navigation with clear icons and a smooth flow.
DMZ has its own separate progression from the rest of the game, featuring 70 levels you can only climb through by playing it. It also, unsurprisingly, has its own separate economy of cash and crafting materials that persist between rounds, essentially making it a game within a game. That said, certain elements - such as weapon progression, are shared with Modern Warfare 4's multiplayer modes and battle royale mode Warzone.
The developer has also ramped up the intensity of AI enemies and widened the number of difficulty tiers to make for a more dynamic enemy distribution across the map. Enemies now exist in four tiers of aggression and power, with the most challenging - Commanders - roaming the map protected by a posse of tough enemies that you'll have to get through first before facing the Commander.
Meta progression is another element that's been expanded upon greatly compared to the 2022 DMZ beta. All players have a home base called the Forward Operating Base (FOB), which you can walk around and explore, including alongside other players in your party. The space is similar to the Hideout in Escape from Tarkov and other extraction shooters, in that it also houses several important interactive stations you'll be using after each run.
At the FOB, you can manage active operators - the characters you can play as - look through your stash, create a loadout, customise your weapons, test them at the firing range, accept missions called Orders and open loot packs. The FOB also has a 3D printer, which uses ingredients gathered from the field to craft useful items.
The FOB also has a vendor that sells weapons and other items for in-game cash, as well as a case to display your collected dog tags, a bounty leaderboard that tracks the top PvP players, and a boss board that provides intel on powerful AI enemies roaming around.
There's quite a bit more in the official DMZ blog post, so give it a read if you're curious about specifics. More blog posts and reveals are expected throughout the week.
DMZ is available at Modern Warfare 4's launch on 23rd October for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2. Infinity Ward recently announced two major changes coming to Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone that have players excited: a silly skin off toggle for Warzone, and a tweak to double XP tokens so they count down in match and not real-time.

item.description:
Creating a timely satire can be tough when development takes half a decade or more - it's the reason South Park's stuck with its crude art style for literal decades, but the developers of GTA 6 can't just replace their world-class tech with paper cutouts. Instead, the team simply tried to avoid trends that would become outdated come launch.
"We work on it for years and years," Rockstar's senior vice president of narrative, Rupert Humphries, told Love Magazine, "so you need to make content that will feel vital to the moment of release. If there's a trend blowing up for six months, you need to see it for what it is and not jump on the bandwagon." While South Park can centre an entire episode on demonic Labubus and squeeze out some laughs while they're still hot, GTA doesn't quite have the same luxury.
Rather than betting on memes that expired years ago, Rockstar leaned into "things that interested us, like conspiracy theories," Humphries added. "The strange ways the public reacts to everyday occurrences, and those are the kinds of things we ran with. In most cases, rather than trying to put a like-for-like of something real in the world, we have created our own slanted, overblown versions, be that a conspiracy theory, or another universal contemporary phenomenon."
Grand Theft Auto's always been a darkly satirical series, but it frequently tackles tougher subjects too. One notable constant is how the series deals with the American Dream and how the public's attitude toward the American Dream has shifted through the years.
Humphries stops short of explaining what GTA 6's take on the American Dream is exactly, but his interpretation might certainly be a clue to Jason and Lucia's motivations. Perhaps they're not chasing excessive, bottomless pools of cash with no end in sight like the GTA protagonists before them. We'll find out when GTA 6 launches next month on the 19th of November.

item.title: Halo Studios can't promise that the previously-announced Halo novel will land on shop shelves, but the company is "determined" to see the project cross the finish line regardless. Read more
item.description:
Halo Studios can't promise that the previously-announced Halo novel will land on shop shelves, but the company is "determined" to see the project cross the finish line regardless.
Xbox's influential sci-fi series is in the middle of a massive shakeup behind the scenes. As part of the console maker's sweeping restructure, mass layoffs hit developer Halo Studios and the entire series moved under Activision's supervision. Xbox's Matt Booty said "a small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market."
Now, franchise writer Alex Wakeford has addressed what's happening with two of the series' upcoming stories - Troy Denning's Halo: Fireteam Noble and Kenneth Peters' Halo: Burn the Road Home novella.
"Many have been asking whether this novel will still be releasing," Wakeford wrote in a recent Halo Waypoint blog post, speaking about Fireteam Noble. "To this we can say that it is absolutely our intent to see this project cross the finish line. Troy has written a fantastic story and a good chunk of the editorial process has been conducted. In my remaining time at the studio, I will be doing all I can to ensure this can be achieved."
As for the newly-revealed novella, Wakeford also said "we are determined to see this through to completion."
Question marks have understandably lingered over multiple Halo-related projects in recent weeks. The studio confirmed that December's Halo Fest event is still going ahead, despite the dramatic shakeup, but Activision's rumored lore reboot had many folks still worried about the future of Fireteam Noble and any other in-development novels, which presumably exist in the current Halo continuity.
Halo: Fireteam Noble was previously set to come out next year and takes place after Halo 5's story. Denning penned several of the best Halo books, and also contributed to Halo: Campaign Evolved's three-mission prequel arc. Details on Burn the Road Home are a little lighter, but a portion of the studio's blog post that was written before the layoffs mentioned it's "dropping out of slipspace next year."
The rest of the Halo Waypoint post includes several never-before-seen pieces of concept art set on Zeta Halo - the ring from Halo Infinite - and shows off biomes that definitely didn't end up in the final game. Perhaps they were made for a follow-up project? I've left a few of them embedded above.
"With that, Canon Fodder has come to an end," Wakeford wrote. "Forever? Who knows, eh? Who knows. Those who come after may well choose to continue it, a new author may yet lend their pen to this series for future narrative endeavors. In such an event we'll take this moment to offer a firm handshake to whoever this future person may be. Go forth and deliver unto the community the good word about all things Halo story and lore… And we have loved this great journey with you all so very, very much."

item.title: Film and TV show adaptations of Arc Raiders and The Finals are in the works - and developer Embark Studios is collaborating with Chernin Entertainment to get the job done. Read more
item.description:
Film and TV show adaptations of Arc Raiders and The Finals are in the works - and developer Embark Studios is collaborating with Chernin Entertainment to get the job done.
Variety reports that a number of production companies were competing for the rights to adapt both hit shooters, but Chernin Entertainment won out a few months after no-clipping into creepypasta land and stumbling upon huge box office success with this year's Backrooms horror film.
The Nexon-owned Embark is supposedly working closely with Chernin "to ensure the creativity that defines both of these properties extends into all-new formats," according to studio CEO Patrick Söderlund, who also told Variety the agreement is the next step in turning both series into "deeply integrated transmedia experiences."
"Arc Raiders and The Finals are exactly the kind of opportunities we've been building towards," Chernin's film president, David Ready, added. "Nexon and Embark have created visually stunning, atmospheric worlds that contain countless stories to tell." There's no word yet on who's directing, writing or starring in any of these projects, however.
Arc Raiders and The Finals join an impossibly large crowd of video games waiting to get the big/small screen treatment. Only a few weeks ago, Sega and Netflix penned a deal to make projects based on Sonic The Hedgehog, Crazy Taxi and the still-unreleased Stranger Than Heaven.
Despite all the game-to-film and game-to-show projects in the pipeline - there's a lot - I'm quite excited at the prospect of an Arc Raiders adaptation. The extraction shooter's massive and imposing robotic stalkers could make for some fun movie monster thrills if done right.
Either way, Arc Raiders has sold over 16m copies since its release a year ago. A free trial (8th to 12th October) is aiming to get even more people in the door, alongside the game's biggest update yet, Frozen Trails. A PvE test is also scheduled for 13th of October to accommodate the shooter's surprisingly friendly scavengers.
