item.description:
So many of the questions in a press briefing for the upcoming Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft book revolved around whether the 52-year-old tabletop game would bend out of shape to work like a massively multiplayer online game. But while the D&D translation of WoW does include races and dungeons and characters from Blizzard's famous game, it doesn't fundamentally alter what it is.
The D&D: World of Warcraft book releases 17th November, and it's a 256-page publication stuffed with quite a lot of new art, and it brings 16 playable species (races) from WoW to D&D. Of those, Dwarf, Elf, Goblin, Human, and Orc were already in D&D, but Dracthyr, Draenei, Earthen, Forsaken, Haranir, Mechagnome, Pandaren, Tauren, Troll, Vulpera, and Worgen are being added.
Similarly, there are new playable subclasses in the shape of Oath of the Ebon Blade and Oath of the Holy Paladin subclasses (the former meant to be a Death Knight-like specialisation); the Demon Hunter Ranger, the Shadow Domain and Discipline Domain Cleric, and the Path of the Elements Barbarian. Other subclasses have been updated for the game: the Sashbuckler Rogue, the Path of the Spiritual Guardian, and the Warrior of Mystic Brews Monk.
There are 60 new spells being added to conjure that WoW feeling, and crafting is being adjusted to introduce professions to D&D. But perhaps more importantly, the entire continent of Azeroth - expansions and all - is there for you to explore and do with as you wish, and there are some incredibly famous characters from the game to play around with. Burning Crusade boss Illidan is there, fallen paladin turned Lich King Arthas is there, Sylvanas is there. And there are all kinds of dungeons to explore, including Dire Maul, Scarlet Monastery, Ragefire Chasm, Shadowfang Keep and more. They've all been reinterpreted slightly to work well in a D&D environment.
For example, there are no raids in D&D: World of Warcraft; there are iconic raid-dungeons such as Onyxia's Lair, but they're encounters for small groups of friends - four or five - rather than 20 or 40. "The joke I always like to make is that most of us have enough trouble getting five people together around a table, let alone 40," principal designer James Wyatt told the assembled group of press, which I was a part of.
Similarly, you won't suddenly be grinding bosses for tiered loot or equipment, because that's not the point of D&D, where you don't wear piecemeal sets of armour and where combat takes much longer. It'd break immersion to fight the same resurrecting character over and over again. Plus, you won't die and resurrect at a Spirit Healer, because that's not how D&D works; even the quintessential WoW faction divide of Horde versus Alliance isn't as hard-written into the tabletop interpretation of the game as it is in computer-game WoW. It's up to the Dungeon Master how prevalent that conflict is.
James Wyatt said the best way to think of the new project as a "paraphrased" version of WoW, rather than a "translation" of it. "I've been trying to shift my thinking to talking about 'paraphrase', because we're not doing a word-for-word translation of any WoW game mechanics," he said. "The game you're sitting down at the table to play is still D&D in the setting of World of Warcraft, and with a lot of the trappings of World of Warcraft, and hopefully evoking the feel of World of Warcraft without making you do the kinds of math calculations that an MMO is doing on your computer chip all the time that you don't have to think about.
There's obviously a lot of inspiration in the book from WoW the video game - that's the whole point of it, and I'll come onto what is there in a moment - "but translating those two directly leads to a really unsatisfying experience", Wyatt said. "D&D players don't grind. They don't fight the same boss over and over again, because that suspends your disbelief and your immersion in the game," he explained.
"So the the goal is to try to evoke the feeling of playing WoW and let you interact with the characters and creatures and abilities that you have as a WoW character, while also opening up the world for you to explore in a whole new way, because you can talk to anybody that you meet, you can interact with anything you see, which is the the beauty of a tabletop game."
Meanwhile, in video game land, World of Warcraft is also having a busy year. Blizzard revealed WoW: Forever at BlizzCon recently, and launched a closed beta for it, which Connor was very enthusiastic about. WoW: Forever takes the game back to its Classic origins but expands upon them with never before seen additions to the game and world, and it intends to veer off in a direction of its own hereafter.

item.title: In a new interview, Rockstar has discussed its revered approach to crafting the satire the Grand Theft Auto series is famous for - particularly relating to GTA 6 and whether the game should include, and lampoon, real-world politics. Read more
item.description:
In a new interview, Rockstar has discussed its revered approach to crafting the satire the Grand Theft Auto series is famous for - particularly relating to GTA 6 and whether the game should include, and lampoon, real-world politics.
Speaking to the Paris-based fashion magazine Love, for a feature story in issue 27, (photographed and spread on X), Rockstar said it favours creating its own world and fictitious events, rather than piggybacking the events in ours. This isn't necessarily because it's protecting its back, but more to make its own world even more ridiculous, and to guard against a game feeling dated by the time it's released.
"If you go back to previous GTAs, there's never really been much focus on national politics," said Rupert Humphries, senior vice president of narrative of Rockstar. "The rise of Homeland Security and the Patriot Act were pretty central to GTA 4, but that was mainly because post-9/11 New York was a real frontline for those issues. Because we are trying to make games that feel very specific to the moment they are released, but at the same time, not reflective of the exact world we live in, we don't want to be too specific about any particular person, event, movement or anything like that.
"Making a game in Florida though, there is so much to work with," Humphries added, "and we have really tried to build out our world - filling it with all the characters and culture wars necessary to make it feel alive. And then we have so many ways to tell these stories outside of actually meeting characters face to face. You can see a sign for an election, receive a robocall from a campaign, or hear a commercial on the radio. And then we have some great political talk shows on the radio too where they discuss all these issues.
"Red Dead Redemption 2 was essentially a historical recreation, with a lot of the same tools we have used to make GTA 6; there is a big focus on not just holding up a mirror, but on making everything satirical, larger than life, and more grotesque. Otherwise, you could just go outside and live in the real world! We try to get to the heart of whatever issue we want to talk about and then explode the part of it we find interesting until the ridiculousness of the position becomes really clear and hopefully funny too."
The other thing to keep in mind, Humphries said, is the game's development time. Rockstar has worked on GTA 6 for "years and years" so it needs to fill the game with events and stories that still feel "vital" when the game is released. "If there's a trend blowing up for six months, you need to see it for what it is and not jump on the bandwagon," Humphries explained.
Were Rockstar simply to try and recreate the world we live in - the sort of approach it used for Red Dead Redemption 2, because that historical period has long passed - it wouldn't be enough. It would be replicating the world outside your window. "It's not interesting," Humphries said. "If you are going to put all this effort into creating a version of today's world, it has to be more over the top, more insane, more in your face."
Rockstar said similar things to IGN in a GTA 6 interview not so long ago, with Rockstar North's Rob Nelson assuring people "there's always stuff to satirise". "As long as humans are humans, other humans will figure out ways to satirise what we do," Nelson said. But Rockstar has to be "careful" what it chooses to satirise such that it doesn't feel "dated" when the game arrives, he stressed, underlining that thinking.
Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives 19th November, which is alarmingly close at hand. It's an enormously ambitious project, pushing the levels of realism and interactivity - sometimes very controversially - that players can expect from a simulated city, while telling a kind of Bonnie and Clyde love story between co-protagonists Jason and Lucia. Indeed, keeping their relationship together appears to be one of your overriding objectives in the game.
But while Rockstar prepares to release what's expected to be its most successful game ever, the company also faces employment-related legal difficulties in the UK, after abruptly firing 31 workers from the Rockstar North studio in Scotland last year. That case - which revolves around allegations of union-busting - is being tried in an employment tribunal right now.

item.title: More bad news for Ninja Theory today, as the studio's consultation process with Xbox - following a second wave of cuts last week - seems to have resulted in layoffs. Read more
item.description:
More bad news for Ninja Theory today, as the studio's consultation process with Xbox - following a second wave of cuts last week - seems to have resulted in layoffs.
First, how did we get here? Back in July, Xbox announced the beginning of its "reset". This is a major restructuring of the Xbox business, and included 3,200 planned job cuts and several studio cuts.
One of those studios was Ninja Theory. Unlike Double Fine - another studio that managed to head off on its own as an independent developer - Xbox had worked to transfer ownership of Ninja Theory to another company. That way, the studio could live on and continue work on Senua, a game only revealed back in June.
Sadly, the proposed sale of Ninja Theory didn't manifest, as a letter penned by Xbox COO Matt Booty confirmed that two separate sale-related agreements "fell through". As a result, Xbox and Ninja Theory began a consultation process as the studio moved towards closure, though Booty was sure to note that Xbox would "continue to explore other paths forward" in the meantime. As such, Ninja Theory's closure wasn't a certainty.
While the wider survival of Ninja Theory remains up in the air, we fast forward to today where its developers nonetheless face redundancy. As spotted by journalist Chris Kerr, employees took to LinkedIn to express their sadness around the situation, as well as their appreciation for their fellow Ninja Theory developers.
"Sadly, after almost nine incredible years at Ninja Theory, my position is now at risk," wrote principle sound designer Daniele Galante. They shared an anecdote about the first Hellblade scene they worked, and then added: "Although I am not going to pretend I am not sad about having to say goodbye to many friends, I feel ready for my next adventure, knowing that I will bring with me a huge wealth of experience gained at Ninja and throughout my previous roles."
Gameplay programmer Katrin Mair posted: "I've been trying to figure out how to write this because Ninja Theory was never just a job to me. I moved to the UK for Ninja. It was where I started my career in the games industry, and it ended up becoming such a big part of my life."
Principle programmer Stefano Prosperi added: "Now, with Ninja Theory facing closure and all of us facing redundancy, it's difficult to process the idea that this chapter may be coming to an end. I feel sadness, uncertainty and disappointment, of course. But more than anything, I feel incredibly fortunate.
"Fortunate to have spent 13 years doing something I love.
Fortunate to have worked with people at the very top of their craft. Fortunate to have been part of a studio that created things we genuinely cared about."
These three are a few of the many developers who have either lost, or are at risk of losing, their jobs as part of Xbox's restructuring. This mass reorganisation has still not concluded, leaving those at other Xbox-owned studios fearful of future cuts.
Ninja Theory in recent years had established itself as a stand-out UK studio, responsible for the acclaimed Hellblade series. Hellblade 2 earned five stars from Eurogamer back in 2024, and was described as "triumphant".

item.description:
Amazingly, the thing that's sold me on Sword Sage: Awakening's potential isn't the adorable red panda deity who poofs out of thin air to serve you restorative tea whenever you rest up at its cheery Soulslike bonfire equivalent - although I'll admit it comes close. As its silly tea-stop interludes suggest, Sword Sage - which joins the rising swell of China-developed Soulslikes drawing inspiration from the country's rich folklore - is doing things a little bit differently. But its most interesting ideas go deeper than mood.
That said, its cheerier tone is probably the thing you'll notice first. Compared to the sombre stylings of your average Soulslike, Sword Sage feels - in my hour-or-so hands-on time, at least - positively buoyant. That starts with its effervescent, pinwheeling protagonist Pei Sanniang - a novice disciple of the Yuangong Sect who, as the demo begins, is returning from a year of wandering. She's an endearing presence, enthusiastically animated, as she bounds up ladders, launches into furiously elegant attacks, and turns bogstandard jumps into silly mid-air twirls.
Pei and the sect specialise in the disposal of yaoguai, malevolent entities from Chinese folklore. And wouldn't you know it, there's a whole bunch of them knocking around as Pei begins her trip along the Cypress Path - a misty mountain pass of verdant greenery, rickety wooden walkways, and, later, cloud-swaddled pagodas skewering bright blue skies. Here, it's gentle birdsong rather than discordant moans that accompany the sound of swirling limbs and dancing blades, and, honestly, it's refreshing to play a Soulslike that isn't so obsessed with perpetual gloom. Whether that lighter tone persists, however, remains to be seen.
As I chart the Cypress Path, I'm funnelled along yaoguai-dotted pathways whose occasional branches afford a brief exploratory detour. Sometimes enemies amble out in the open, other times there's a bit of FromSoftware-style cheekiness to their placement - dogs tucked inside shadowy cavemouths that tempt passersby with glistening treasures, or yaoguai hiding under ledges so you get a surprise sword in the back as you drop on down. Every so often, I stumble upon a shortcut I can use to loop back to an earlier area of the otherwise fairly linear path. And at irregular intervals, a glowing kettle lantern indicates a place to summon Rosy Roundhound's impromptu tea shop, where I can rest, restore my limited elixirs, and reset the world.
So far, so Soulslike (tea panda aside), but it's a pacier sort of action-RPG too. There are no runbacks, for instance: XP is earned by completing quests and defeating yaoguai. And as you accrue enough, it's automatically turned into merits you can spend on upgrades sprawled across a busy skill tree. Nor is developer Sword Panda Games pitching its difficulty toward relentless punishment. Players who struggle to adapt to Sword Sage's idiosyncratic combat rhythms, or who find themselves at a boss-shaped impasse, will, I'm told, be granted various reprieves. And while we're talking combat, it's here I'm properly intrigued.
Pei's basic attacks comes from her exuberant swordplay; a rapid succession of slashes that gradually drain an enemy's Vital Energy until their defenses are down. This opens them up to a powerful Vital Strike capable of significant damage. She can also break enemy shields and cancel their defensive stances with a swirling kick, or block incoming attacks to negate damage at the expense of weapon durability. Weapons break quickly in Sword Sage, and when they do they can no longer block and only cause minimal damage. But before you roll your eyes, this isn't anywhere near as wearying as it might sound. Weapons can be reforged and restored to full strength, with a satisfying clank and whir, near-instantaneously at the press of a button. As such, weapon breakage is a minor inconvenience, but, crucially, adds an unusual secondary rhythm to a combat system that already has a distinctive flow.
And it's all about that flow. Sword Sage's big differentiator is its evasion system. Familiar rolls are replaced by Evade Cyan dodges and Strike Red counters. Hold the block button and tap the right stick at just the right moment and you'll escape harm. But match your evade to the direction of an enemy's attack - pressing up to avoid a high strike, tapping left or right to slide around mid-level attacks, or flicking down to avoid low ones - and Pei performs a dodge followed by a powerful follow-up counter.
But there's more to consider. You've got boon-granting talismans, craftable consumable relics including throwing knives and supernaturally enhanced firecrackers, and you can switch between two equipped weapons at any time (these appear to consist of a pool of standard 'types' that drop with randomised skill bonuses and stats as you play). All together, it makes for enjoyably balletic carnage with a satisfying rhythm of its own.
Basic grunts don't, admittedly, require Pei to flex her abilities too much, but that gradually changes as my demo goes on. One memorable encounter, for instance, involves two yaoguai; one with a massive shield and the other with a fondness for springboarding off it into a powerful dive, requiring a complicated bit of crowd management to keep them separated long enough to defeat them. Elsewhere, a red-headed mini-boss with a big sword, a love of booze, and the gut to prove it, highlights the importance of Strike Reds as you attempt to whittle down his Vital Energy gauge so you can properly open him up to attack. Still later, I stumble upon a monk-like mini-boss that tosses out throwing projectiles and frantic follow-up slashes so fast, my evade-counter-reforge-attack timing gets its first real workout.
But it's not until the demo's first big boss that Sword Sage's combat elements really start to coalesce and I get a clearer sense of how encounters might evolve. Like Pei, the towering Fangxiang Exorcist is a wonderfully characterful bit of design, jigging from toe-to-toe as he waves around some sort of spooky rock. Sometimes he swings from the side or grasps with his claws; other times he'll do a powerful overhead pound sending shockwaves across the floor.
He's also got a sizable Vital Energy pool to deplete, and goes big on the unblockable critical attacks - meaning directional evades are essential for survival, while follow-up counters are necessary to prevent the battle dragging on so long your restoratives have entirely depleted. In other words, he's a formidable adversary; a proper test for my fledgling fighting skills and the first time I'm really forced to observe and respond at speed, to adopt a more instinctual approach to evasion and reforge timing. And it makes for an enjoyable dance.
Fangxiang Exorcist feels like a strong place to end my demo then, piquing my curiosity for the adventure to follow. And on that front, Sword Panda says Sword Sage: Awakening should take between 12-18 hours to complete, depending on a player's thoroughness, as its three chapters unfold. Each chapter promises four bosses between the various branching routes forward, while the third, intriguingly, is said to switch things up with a more open, go-anywhere sandbox style of play. There's no release date for Sword Sage yet, but when it does show up it'll be on PC and PS5 - and Sword Panda hopes to eventually add Xbox and Switch 2 to the list too. I'll be keeping my eye on this one, and not just because of the panda.
This preview is based on a hands-on presentation at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. 4Divinity provided flights and accommodation.

item.title: Behaviour Interactive, the Canadian studio mostly known for asymmetrical multiplayer horror survival game Dead by Daylight, is hiring for a new project that sounds altogether different. Read more
item.description:
Behaviour Interactive, the Canadian studio mostly known for asymmetrical multiplayer horror survival game Dead by Daylight, is hiring for a new project that sounds altogether different.
A job posting on Behaviour's website (via Insider Gaming) for a senior technical animator reveals the studio is hiring for an unannounced "triple-A Sci-Fi FPS" being built using Unreal Engine. The post describes the shooter as having "a high realism bar".
Behaviour's main game over the last decade has been Dead by Daylight, which recently celebrated its 10th anniversary by setting a new Steam concurrent player record. The studio, however, has developed other projects for third-party publishers. Recent examples include Serious Sam: Shatterverse, Monopoly: Star Wars Heroes vs. Villains and the mobile game Worms Across Worlds.
In 2023, Behaviour self-published Meet Your Maker, a building game where the goal is to invade other players' created fortresses to steal loot. The game featured a wide array of traps and other tools creative players could use to devise the most evil contraptions.
Unfortunately, despite a promising start, the game just wasn't successful enough for Behaviour to maintain it long term. The studio announced in 2024, nearly one year after launch, that it's essentially shifting into maintenance mode as the game's team moved on to other projects.
Behaviour has one other upcoming project that we know about: the recently announced Exterminauts, a co-op PvE shooter where three players take on alien creatures using repurposed weapons and tools. Exterminauts is a third-person shooter, however, ruling it out. It does not yet have a release date.

item.title: Player numbers are still rising for The Witcher 3 following the release of the Remastered edition upgrade last week, as people not only return to the game following its overhaul but also buy it for the first time, or again. Read more
item.description:
Player numbers are still rising for The Witcher 3 following the release of the Remastered edition upgrade last week, as people not only return to the game following its overhaul but also buy it for the first time, or again.
Over the weekend - specifically yesterday, Sunday 4th October at 4pm BST, according to SteamDB - The Witcher 3 set a new Steam concurrent player record of 137,724. That's a nearly 20K improvement over the game's previous high of 120K players.
For reference: The Witcher 3 attracted 92K concurrent players when it launched in 2015, and had a previous peak of 103K in January 2020, when The Witcher Netflix show was popular. This is good news for game-maker CD Projekt Red, of course, which is seeing first-hand how much pulling power its fantasy game still has, ahead of its new Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past arriving next year at some point.
These numbers don't include console players, either, meaning total player-numbers across PlayStation, Xbox and Switch are presumably much higher. How much higher, we don't know officially, though Alinea Analytics has provided some guidance. Last week, a day after the Remastered edition's release, Alinea analyst Rhys Elliott said The Witcher 3 spiked at 2.4 million daily active users across PC, PlayStation and Xbox (Switch wasn't included for some reason).
"Perhaps even more impressively," Elliott added, "The Witcher 3 sold another 130K copies across those three platforms YESTERDAY [30th September], the most it's sold in a day since The Witcher 3's first $3.99 Steam discount price back in summer 2024. It's currently on sale for $24.99 across all three platforms I'm covering here. Almost $3M in revenue!"
As Elliott noted, that puts Witcher 3 lifetime sales over 66m copies now. "What a run," Elliott said.
The Witcher 3 - Remastered is a significant, free overhaul of the existing game that not only modernises the graphical look of the game, right down to its textures, but also improves animations and reworks the game's skills and skill tree. The Witcher 3 - Remastered is, as I wrote last week, an extraordinarily generous offering, though there are teething problems surrounding lighting and other issues that CD Projekt Red is rolling hotfixes out for.

item.title: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve has joined the ranks of September-October releases that have done very well commercially. The sequel, which officially launched on 2nd October following three days of early access, has been very popular on Steam. Read more
item.description:
Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve has joined the ranks of September-October releases that have done very well commercially. The sequel, which officially launched on 2nd October following three days of early access, has been very popular on Steam.
According to SteamDB, Ace Combat 8 peaked at a respectable 52,694 concurrent players. The figure was achieved on Saturday, one day after Friday's official launch. Although we have no visibility on PlayStation and Xbox player numbers, it's hard to imagine them being anything but equal, at the very least.
Ace Combat has historically been console-first. Most games in the series were never released on PC, so it's good to see it thriving on Steam. The renaissance started with 2019's Ace Combat 7: Skies Unknown, which released on PC days after PS4 and Xbox One and peaked at 13,758 concurrent players on Steam. Though that number seems modest today, it was Ace Combat's biggest debut on PC at that point. This is what makes Ace Combat 8's jump in player numbers all the more commendable.
Players appear to be happy, too, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Very Positive with over 5,755 reviews. This follows a brief controversy that erupted shortly after the game's early access launch where players were disappointed to find Ace Combat Zero: The Belkan War, a pre-order bonus, is not a standalone app as they were lead to believe and has to instead be launched through Ace Combat 8, creating a lot of unnecessary problems. Bandai Namco has since apologised for the misleading wording on the store, and vowed to explore potential solutions.

item.description:
Final Fantasy Resonance, a game made from the ashes of closed-down mobile game Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, is good. Very good, in fact, as I learned at Gamescom 2026. It's basically a pixel-first FF RPG that takes old-school turn-based combat and modernises it. It feels like Octopath Traveler, but with all the classic Final Fantasy stuff in there, supported by some stunning HD-2D sprite work that looks simply divine.
I have been thinking about the game since Gamescom, sinking five hours into the free demo that launched shortly afterwards. It's a great, modern reinterpretation of what 'classic' Final Fantasy looks like - and it turns out that was Square Enix's intention all along, Final Fantasy Resonance director Hiroto Furuya told Kotaku in an interview. "As a foundation, it’s very important [that] we have knowledge of Final Fantasy's history and its past. But we're also gamers at heart, so of course we play the latest games that are available outside of Final Fantasy. We have the sensibility of knowing Final Fantasy's history, as well as the general feeling of playing more modern games".
Furuya went on to talk about the specific games the team has looked at when rethinking the combat system from Brave Exvius, considering how a pixel-first Final Fantasy should feel and play in the modern age. And it turns out the best place to look for inspiration were the last two pixel Final Fantasy titles in the mainline series: 1992's Final Fantasy 5 and 1994's Final Fantasy 6.
"The first concept we had in mind, simply put, is what if we take the job system from Final Fantasy 5 and the unique characteristics of each character in Final Fantasy 6, what would that look like?" Resonance producer Keisuke Nakashima told Kotaku. "This type of experiment hasn't been done in the past, so it required a bit of research and innovation."
Nakashima went on to discuss how the studio examined the strengths and weaknesses of the stagger system - a modern mechanic present in the FF7 Remake series and FF16, that requires you inflict a certain amount of 'stamina' damage to enemies in order to interrupt their turns - and incorporated that into the retro inspirations from the 90s games. "[That combination] ultimately [formed] into what you see now, where you have these distinct characteristics, but it also allows for that additional customisation element," said Nakashima.
For my money, the balance is great: by having a cast of characters with their own skills and abilities and pairing them with 'Visions' (characters from the series' past with their own unique abilities), you have a lot of variation across your team, and many combat puzzles with plenty of ways to tackle them. From the demo(es) I've played, I can see this having a lot of potential for RPG fanatics, and a really refreshing injection of turn-based brainteasing for the Final Fantasy series. Given how integral the 'Visions' are to the game's identity and combat mechanics, it's surprising to learn that - at one point - the team considered shipping the game without them.
"There was a time in development where we explored leaving the Final Fantasy series characters out," said Furuya. "However, we ultimately landed on incorporating them, even though there is difficulty in intermixing their worldview with ours. When you go back to the point of how cool it would be to use Cloud’s Cross-Slash, and the bombastic CG sequences, it really delivers on the spectacle and fun that we were drawn to."
Safe to say, I'm excited for this game. Final Fantasy Resonance launches on 22nd October on PC (Steam), PS5, Switch 2, and Xbox Series X/S.

item.title: RuneScape creator Jagex recently hosted its annual convention RuneFest, a hub for community events and new reveals for the British developer's many games. Sadly, one of those reveals has spoilt the fun somewhat due to unexpected generative AI use. Read more
item.description:
RuneScape creator Jagex recently hosted its annual convention RuneFest, a hub for community events and new reveals for the British developer's many games. Sadly, one of those reveals has spoilt the fun somewhat due to unexpected generative AI use.
The trailer, a cinematic reveal for RuneScape 3's Dragon Slayer 2 quest, presents the premise for a new big adventure in a sketched style. However, people quickly spotted some strange issues with this trailer, such as a hand with six fingers, and a pair of fantasy Air Jordans.
Players were immediately angry about the use of generative AI for this trailer. Jagex staff had only reaffirmed its stance against generative AI use only a few days ago when a third-party apparel collaboration received flak for its use of gen AI in its design. When that happened, Jagex Sween responded on Reddit, posting: "We're as angry as you are about this. We wouldn't have approved the use of AI in any designs. We don't use generative AI to replace the artists and developers who make our games, we don't use it in our marketing materials, and we won't use it in our merchandising or allow its use in partnerships.RuneScape, all of our games, is built by talented people, and that human craft and creativity matters enormously to us."
This latest trailer coming in such short succession then isn't a good look for the developer, nor its stance against generative AI. Another statement was released in the wake of this trailer backlash, one that echoes much of the frustration from irked community members.
"We’re aware of the concerns raised about the Dragon Slayer 2 trailer and have taken it down, while we investigate urgently. This trailer was produced by a trusted external partner who had explicitly confirmed that GenAI would not be used. But, among other things, there’s a sixth finger and, well, that’s pretty hard to explain away. For that we apologise.
"Our position is clear at Jagex: we don’t use GenAI to create our games, artwork or creative assets, and will not knowingly allow it to be used on our behalf. This is the second time in quick succession that concerns about generative AI have arisen through partners we trusted, and for us that highlights an issue with our own processes which we must address.
"Immediately following RuneFest we’re overhauling our review processes, and we’re going to work with and commission creators from the community to make sure that the story of Dragon Slayer II is told to the standard befitting of such an update."
It's a bit of a pie-in-the-face moment, for sure. Still, one lives and learns, and if it leads to a new system of careful collaboration and quality assurance of third-party partnerships for the company, maybe that's a good thing. As an olive branch to the RuneScape players, maybe they should add (legally distinct) Rune Air Jordans as a new Beginner Clue scroll reward? Just an idea.
Other Jagex trailers revealed at Runefest proved much more exciting, such as the announcement of a Reignited version of Runescape with new HD visuals, and a whole new Runescape MMO in development.

item.description:
Arc Raiders studio Embark is making the extraction shooter free to play for four days alongside the launch of the game's biggest update yet, Frozen Trail. The studio spent the last few days detailing all the new aspects of the update, and has now announced a way for players curious about the game to try it out.
The trial runs 8th to 12th October. Arc Raiders will be free to download and play across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox during that period. The trial surprisingly doesn't feature any locked content, with Embark saying it "grants access to the full Arc Raiders game".
That also extends to the new Pendola Pass map, which free weekend players can technically access immediately. That said, because the map needs to be unlocked by progressing through levels, it may take you a while to get there. Failing that, you can have a friend who already has Pendola Pass unlocked invite you to their squad.
Frozen Trail is expected to be a major moment for Arc Raiders. The expansion-size update adds a massive new map, several new Arc enemies and new weapons and gadgets. The update also marks the first major overhaul of the metagame, with tweaks to ammo, crafting and the addition of a more standard battle pass.
Arc Raiders has long since lost its massive launch audience, but I could see Frozen Trail being enough of a reason to lure players back. Given how much of the core game the update changes, Embark likely also sees it as the best entry point for new players.
Incidentally, right after the free trial concludes, Arc Raiders will be hosting a PvE test to give anyone who doesn't want to fight other players what they've been asking for since the game launched. The test runs 13th to 20th October, and simply disables player-on-player damage, essentially formalising the attitude of the game's famously friendly lobbies.

item.title: Dynasty Warriors producer Tomohiko Sho says he'd rather spend what's left of his career making new games than more remasters of his old ones. Read more
item.description:
Dynasty Warriors producer Tomohiko Sho says he'd rather spend what's left of his career making new games than more remasters of his old ones.
Sho isn't ruling future remasters out entirely, but he's not volunteering for the job either. Asked by 4Gamer (machine-translated) about the prospect shortly after Dynasty Warriors 3 Complete Edition Remastered launched on Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S, he made it clear that whether or not the series gets another remaster depends on how well this release performs, and hinted he'd personally prefer not to be the one making it.
"I can't say anything at the moment, and I haven't even thought about it, but it's not impossible that we'll remaster titles that aren't available on Steam," he said (thanks, IG).
"However, to be honest, I don't want to do it. It would be almost a complete remake, and even this time I sometimes thought, 'Why am I remaking something I made myself?' I'm in my fifties now, and I sometimes think about 'how many more games can I make before I retire', so I'd rather make new games or sequels."
However, he's not against future remasters, either. Sho says he still feels an obligation to the fans who want more remasters, and hints he may hand the job to someone else on the team while he gets on with new games and sequels.
Dynasty Warriors 3 Complete Edition Remastered freshens up the original PlayStation 2 game, one of the franchise's earliest entries, in Unreal Engine 5 to mark its 25th anniversary. It's out now on Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Steam reviews currently suggest fan feedback has been 'Very Positive'.

item.title: Long-time mod makers are not happy about the latest trend to take over their corner of the internet - the "bullshit 'trend'" of AI-generated, or "vibe-coded", mods. Read more
item.description:
Long-time mod makers are not happy about the latest trend to take over their corner of the internet - the "bullshit 'trend'" of AI-generated, or "vibe-coded", mods.
As first reported by IGN, the backlash is building after a number of modders - including some who openly admit to using generative AI to help write their mods - opened up about mashup mods splicing entirely unrelated games together.
we ain't in north shire anymorewow x waw https://t.co/umspoyvHyK pic.twitter.com/fQe03iEnpQ
"I mod games and I'm not shy about the fact that I use AI to do it. I hate this bullshit 'trend'. Pure slop, there's nothing creative about this at all," modder kran27_ posted, adding that "the shit that's getting the clicks is this jingling keys bullshit".
Another, discountmodder, added: "If this becomes the permanent state of modding, this may be my last project. I don't wanna be involved in an AI slop-factory".
Presenting... Escape from Skyrim lol.I put Tarkov into Skyrim. Now with guns and everything you would expect. pic.twitter.com/byFCnvwcbq
What's got them so riled up is the huge surge of mods that bring unrelated games together, from World of Warcraft into Call of Duty: World at War, to Escape From Tarkov into Skyrim, and a version of Insomniac's Spider-Man that lets you swing around Batman: Arkham City's Gotham.
The trend has snowballed just over the course of a single week, driven by Claude Opus 5.5's cheaper tokens and improved code generation making it easier than ever to point the model at a game, decompile it, and add in something else entirely.
Passthrough mods are low-key insane. Legit one of the most fun use cases for AI in a while pic.twitter.com/2JKWBhopMC
The results are inconsistent at best. Footage from YouTuber Brendan Jowett comparing Opus 5.5 against OpenAI's Astra 6 model shows both struggling with the basics, including enemies that ignore the player, a space fighter that flies diagonally while shooting straight ahead.
None of these mashups have popped up on modding platforms like Nexus Mods yet, though, and IGN suggests that's likely down to rights issues rather than lack of interest. Nexus's own 2023 policy on AI-generated content is blunt about it: "In order to prevent any issues with your mods, we encourage you to avoid using these tools unless you have explicit permission to use all the assets".
Almost all of the mods circulating on Twitter/X rely on decompiled code and assets the people building them have no rights to, which is precisely the scenario Nexus's policy was written to exclude.
As IGN posits, whether that holds once a platform does decide to host them is what's got modders most on edge. Right now, the trend is confined to engagement farming on Twitter/X but could reshape what "modding" means.
In related news, ahead of the bottomless GTA 6 mods we'll surely get whenever the crime epic finally comes to PC, Rockstar Games has imposed new restrictions on the modding community.

item.title: PlatinumGames president Atsushi Inaba has hinted he'd like to expand the character of Bayonetta and broaden her world. Read more
item.description:
PlatinumGames president Atsushi Inaba has hinted he'd like to expand the character of Bayonetta and broaden her world.
While he stopped short of confirming a new game, Famitsu reports that when Inaba sat down with Shift Up CEO and Stellar Blade director Kim Hyung-tae during Tokyo Game Show held to mark a crossover bringing four Bayonetta-themed costumes to Stellar Blade Complete Edition on Switch 2 this November, he admitted he still had a desire to expand the franchise further.
Kim used the opportunity to gush about the series himself, calling Bayonetta "an indispensable work in my life" (albeit via machine-translation) and naming it one of his three favourite games, while admitting he had to control himself while designing his own Bayonetta-inspired "Black Dress" costume so it wouldn't go too far. He even asked, half-joking, to design characters for the next entry himself.
Asked directly about that next entry, Inaba declined to give specifics, telling Famitsu only to wait and see.
It's certainly more optimistic than recent conversations - series creator Hideki Kamiya left Platinum in October 2023, saying at the time he'd envisioned Bayonetta as a nine-part saga he may now take "to the grave" with him - and Bayonetta 3 director Yusuke Miyata has also since departed.
If she does come back, it won't be with her iconic Japanese voice work as the series recently lost Bayonetta's Japanese voice actress Atsuko Tanaka, who died in August 2024 aged 61.

item.title: Jagex is offering long-time, lapsed, and new RuneScape players a clean slate with RuneScape Reignited. Read more
item.description:
Jagex is offering long-time, lapsed, and new RuneScape players a clean slate with RuneScape Reignited.
Announced at the same RuneFest 2026 event where Jagex revealed its fourth RuneScape MMO built in Unreal Engine, RuneScape Reignited is a new permanent character type launching on 2 December.
Jagex outlined the details in a blog post entitled "RuneScape As It Was Always Meant To Be", explaining how Reignited characters come with a brand-new economy and hiscores with no paid progression available.
"It plays out in the same worlds that all existing characters are already playing in, and all Reignited characters will have free access to members' content for the first 10 days following its launch," Jagex explained.
"If you've ever felt lost or left behind in RuneScape, or have been unsure of how to come back or where to begin... There genuinely has never been a better time to jump back in or to experience the full adventure from the start – so we've made a reason to do just that," the team wrote.
"Reignited is the culmination of everything that we have been building towards this year, and yet it is also the start of a brand new chapter."
For new players, the game will provide an opportunity to "experience 25 years of RuneScape, from a new shared starting point", while existing players get to "see your worlds thriving again and helping the community grow in all directions. Just as how Ironman players live among existing players today, Reignited characters will be part of your experience inside Gielinor every day".
RuneScape Reignited, The Adventure Guide and the next leap for Remastering RuneScape, will "all arrive in a single update" on 2nd December.
Jagex has also announced a fourth MMO in the RuneScape series. Revealed at RuneFest in Birmingham, the developer announced the new instalment has been built in Unreal Engine. It also confirmed a new RuneScape animated adaptation, made in partnership with YouTuber Charlie "MoistCr1TiKaL" White, is on the way.
A clone of Old School RuneScape briefly appeared on the internet this week, until, stoking the ire of the RuneScape community before being a quickly shut down.

item.title: Jagex has announced a fourth MMO in the RuneScape series. Read more
item.description:
Jagex has announced a fourth MMO in the RuneScape series.
After revealing the new game at RuneFest in Birmingham over the weekend, the developer also announced a new RuneScape animated adaptation, made in partnership with YouTuber Charlie "MoistCr1TiKaL" White, is also on the way.
You can see the reveal teaser below:
According to the studio's own blurb, the game will "bring the world of Gielinor to life in Unreal Engine, combining the depth, freedom and community-led spirit that have defined RuneScape for 25 years with the technology and game design possibilities of today".
The new MMO, currently going by the working title RS4, is still in early development, with Jagex saying it's at least a few years from release and has yet to settle on an official name.
A numbered sequel might seem like the obvious name given RuneScape's history. The game was rebranded RuneScape 2 in 2004 and RuneScape 3 in 2013 before Jagex abandoned numbering altogether, folding everything back into a single live service. These days, the RuneScape stable also includes Old School RuneScape and spin-off RuneScape: Dragonwilds, both still active and separate from whatever RS4 eventually becomes.
Jagex hasn't committed to calling the new game RuneScape 4, numbered or otherwise.
In a blog post, Jagex explained why it had announced RS4 this far ahead of launch, revealing engine and tooling work from Dragonwilds gave the team something to build on, and the studio wanted to extend the same collaborative, community-driven development it's used on RuneScape and Old School.
None of that comes at the expense of the existing games, Jagex said, each of which keeps its own team and its own ongoing investment.
"We'll be designing RS4 to sit alongside them as an additional way to experience RuneScape and the world of Gielinor," Jagex said, adding that "the ambition isn't to replace the RuneScape games you love. It's to make the RuneScape universe bigger".
The new MMO will be set in Gielinor's Sixth Age, beginning in Ashenfall, a region first introduced in RuneScape: Dragonwilds, located to the north-east of the main map.
According to Jagex, RS4 picks up years after Dragonwilds' story and the defeat of the Dragon Queen Kuldra, though the studio says Ashenfall is "only the beginning," with plans to expand "far beyond" it over time into both familiar and new areas of Gielinor.
As for the RuneScape animated adaptation? That's in the works with Charlie White (MoistCr1TiKaL) and LA production company Lyrical Media, aiming to bring "the world, characters and stories of Gielinor to life". It expects to draw from 25 years of history and more than 300 million player accounts created since RuneScape first launched.
A clone of Old School RuneScape briefly appeared on the internet this week, before - stoked the ire of the RuneScape community - it was quickly shut down.

item.description:
As I throw open the windows on my first day in Nivalis, breathing in the city's neon-streaked air and watching the smog roil across the blackened sky, my government-mandated AI automata informs me the district is in lockdown and a serial killer's on the loose. Five hours later, I've become embroiled in a child trafficking plot (the good kind, apparently, seeing as I'm helping them get out); I've stumbled across an oil rig and befriended its city separatists; I've inadvertently struck up a romance with a CorpSec agent who's trying to shut down my noodle bar; and I've met a woman who writes new childhoods for condemned criminals, in the city's hope that implanting them will make 'em behave. All this and I've only grown a single onion. Nivalis Nights, it's fair to say, is not your average farm-life sim.
It is, though, kind of fascinating as it starts from a familiar point and begins building outward. It's also, for context, the follow-up to developer Ion Lands' enjoyable neo-noir delivery adventure Cloudpunk, taking that game's stylish dystopia and reimagining it as the setting for a sort of mash-up of Cyberpunk 2077, Stardew Valley, and Dave the Diver. It's an odd mix, certainly, but it works.
A lot of its early success is down to Nivalis itself. Cloudpunk's city was mostly designed to be viewed from afar, but Nivalis Nights plays out in first-person, demanding a world that can withstand closer scrutiny. And Ion Lands more than rises to the challenge. This Nivalis might still be a world built from jagged pixel-art edges, but it's a richly detailed, wonderfully evocative one (stubbornly wonky framerate aside); a chance to live your own little Blade Runner life, right down to the Vangelis-inspired soundtrack.
But you barely have a minute to admire the way the hazy neon light cuts through the smog on your first day in Nivalis before your automata Ava summons you to the city's culinary centre, Meridian Market. A short taxi ride later, amid the endless bustle and colour, you're the somewhat begrudging new owner of a noodle bar, its previous manager saddling you with all of its debt as a parting gift too. This run-down food stand with its solely al fresco dining set-up is now your problem, but you've at least inherited its cook. And so, across Nivalis Nights' first few days, a crash course in entrepreneurship begins.
That starts with a trip to the furniture shop for a couple of new dining tables and chairs. More space means more customers; more customers means more cash. But more customers also means dwindling ingredients, so it's off to the market you go. Meanwhile, your cook is splitting duties between the kitchen and front-of-house; taking orders, making orders, serving them up. But unfettered business growth is mandatory in this corporate-governed hellhole, and before long, you'll be bolstering your menu, upgrading your decor, and hiring new staff - better cooks, more waiters, cleaners, even managers to look after the day-to-day tasks - so that customers stay happy and the cash continues to flow. Soon, you'll be thinking about wages, schedules and staff morale; you'll inherit a downtown greenhouse where you can grow crops, make cheese, manufacture meat substitutes, and cut out the marketstall middle men. Perhaps you'll start a second business; maybe even open a nightclub too.
For all its cyberpunk ambience, Nivalis Nights' loop of expansion is a pretty familiar one. Yet while the money does seem to flow a little faster if I'm at the noodle bar pitching in, it's surprising how little time I'm apparently expected to be hands-on with the business stuff. Take a taxi to Lowtown, a skytrain to Eastern Residential, or even a boat to the Stacks, and Ion Lands seems determined to distract. Down at the docks, there's a sudden leftfield lurch into vaguely Dave the Diver territory once some grizzled sailorbot hands over his rusty old trawler, leaving me free to chart the city's churning waters in search of exotic fish or ancient plunder. Which, if you're wondering, is how I stumble upon that separatist oil rig.
And I certainly wasn't expecting to see so much story seeded throughout Nivalis. Early on, I meet an old woman convinced her dead husband's personality has been uploaded into a hooverbot, which begins a new side quest. I chase him down, and get to decide whether to keep his secret or rat him out. Several hours later, I've got a hacker on speeddial, a burgeoning friendship with Danny Danetti at his doughnut shop (although my new CorpSec agent "pal" wants me to put an end to that), and I've somehow agreed to train Spartacus Doom in the art of bare metal boxing. And that serial killer thing? I suspect our paths will soon cross.
At this point, I've amassed a veritable shopping list of side quests - so much so I've barely even contemplated a carrot in hours - all accompanied by fully voiced dialogue you can subtly nudge in different directions, stoking romance perhaps, or an air of general disdain. And I've not even mentioned the nighttime swerves into stealth if you choose to break curfew and embark on a more nefarious path. To, say, rob your competitors blind while they sleep.
Truthfully, I haven't really figured out how all these disparate bits fit together, and how Nivalis Nights will evolve as the tutorials die down and it settles into its more regular rhythm. Or even if it'll manage to remain compelling as noodle bar ownership makes way for the more extravagant demands of a full-on business empire - which appears to be the end goal. And there are some niggling issues: that untameable framerate for one, some odd bugs, and a UI that's a touch too fiddly, a touch tempermental, with overbearing overlays and waypoint markers that aren't exactly helpful. But even so, it's enormously refreshing to sink into a life sim that doesn't try and suffocate me with tweeness, and that doesn't leave me dreaming deliriously of turnips.
Yesterday, when I woke up for another day of entrepreneurial toil, storm clouds had gathered and the rain was ASMRing gently against my apartment window. Far below, crowds milled beneath translucent umbrellas and the rain-drenched streets had all but vanished in the mirrored neon glow. And as I splashed toward a flying taxi, Vangelis synths beginning to swell, I thought: for now at least, this weird little dystopia feels like home.

item.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi has responded to fans asking for a full disc version of the game, saying he "did [his] best" to push for physical media as the industry edges towards an all-digital future. Read more
item.description:
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi has responded to fans asking for a full disc version of the game, saying he "did [his] best" to push for physical media as the industry edges towards an all-digital future.
Speaking to Radio Times, as spotted by IGN, Hamaguchi explained his own attachment to physical media, from buying games as a child to wanting friends and colleagues in the industry to sign copies of their work.
"Personally, obviously, I bought lots of physical editions of games as a child. Sometimes I buy digital editions of games, but if I'm particularly attached to a title, I want to get the physical version," he said, adding that the topic has become "particularly sensitive" in recent months.
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will ship with a disc option when it launches in 2027, but PS5 and Xbox Series X players popping in a physical copy will still need to download a hefty chunk of the game to play it in full.
Hamaguchi acknowledged the disc included is a "key disc" containing only the game's opening, and that he understands why some fans have said "no disc, no purchase".
"As the director, it's my responsibility to look after the content of the game to make sure it's fun, really exciting," he said. "The product line-up, the SKUs, how it's going on sale - that is the responsibility of the publishing team. So my authority there is somewhat limited."
Despite that, Hamaguchi said he used his position to argue for a physical version "as much as possible", leading to negotiations "both internally and with first parties" that resulted in the one-disc approach ultimately shipping with the game.
"I completely understand there are those out there who may not really agree with that direction," he said. "But I would just say that I hope you understand that I completely see where you're coming from, and that I did my best. It is a very tricky subject."
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation launches on Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S on 8th April 2027. Hamaguchi said he still expects "physical media will remain in some form going forward", pointing to the continued strength of PC digital sales, but added he can "see a world in the not-too-distant future where physical media is essentially disc-less", reduced to little more than a code printed on paper inside the box.
Sony announced on 1st July it was ceasing production of discs for PlayStation games, effective January 2028. Beyond that point, PlayStation games will be available digitally only. Notably, PlayStation games will continue to be sold at retail, just without a physical disc.
While Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth was "difficult" to Platinum by "design", sequel Revelation's Platinum trophy will be "easier to get".

item.description:
Sony is reportedly in talks to acquire a big-screen adaptation of Electronic Arts' Battlefield, with Christopher McQuarrie attached to write, direct and produce, and Michael B. Jordan on board to produce.
Jordan, fresh off his Best Actor Oscar win, could also end up starring in the film, though Variety notes that's dependent on several factors. Additional producers named include EA's Jesse Stern, Emerald Neon's Carter Swan, Vertigo's Roy Lee and Miri Yoon, and Outlier Society's Elizabeth Raposo.

Resurgence takes place on dedicated maps that are far smaller than the main mode's large playground, and offers many ways to respawn after death. item.title: UPDATED 7TH OCTOBER: A previous version of this story suggested Capcom was evolving RE Engine into an "AI-generation game engine", which is incorrect. Eurogamer has since clarified with a Japanese-speaking colleague that the correct translation is that Capcom is moving "towards a game engine for the AI generation", instead. Read more
item.description:
UPDATED 7TH OCTOBER: A previous version of this story suggested Capcom was evolving RE Engine into an "AI-generation game engine", which is incorrect. Eurogamer has since clarified with a Japanese-speaking colleague that the correct translation is that Capcom is moving "towards a game engine for the AI generation", instead.
We're sorry to have misrepresented what Capcom programmer Satoshi Ishida said. Eurogamer has updated the story to reflect the correct translation below.
ORIGINAL STORY 3RD OCTOBER: Capcom has outlined several ways it wants to evolve its in-house RE engine in the future, including modifying it for an "AI generation" by making it easier for AI to read and understand.
Capcom programmer Satoshi Ishida outlined the intended changes during the Capcom Open Conference RE:2026 event at the weekend (as reported by gamebiz and spotted by VGC), explaining - via machine translation - that the changes were coming as part of an ongoing overhaul dubbed the REX Project.
RE Engine has been in development since 2014 and made its debut in Resident Evil 7 back in 2017. It's since been the engine behind the best part of 30 Capcom titles.
Ishida pointed to three challenges driving the REX Project – one, games have grown so large in scope and data volume that build and iteration times are slowing development down; two, RE Engine is now used by over 2,000 developers, including international staff and people coming from other engines, requiring better multilingual and accessibility support; and three, AI needs to be built into the development pipeline rather than bolted on.
That's why Capcom intends to bundle several new systems into the REX Project, including RE:Dox, which standardises data processing across formats, RE:UI, which speeds up development tools by separating appearance from state, and RE:Log, which swaps text-based logging for an ID-based system.
He also talked about RE:Flows, a visual scripting tool that automatically converts to standard code; and RE:Runtime, a reworked runtime core built around batch processing for large numbers of characters, alongside a new optimised execution layer called RE:C++.
Ishida's goal is to create an engine where AI can understand and generate code, run automated test plays to catch bugs, and support development directly, working towards what he called a future where teams "create games together with AI". Capcom says it has already open-sourced some of the underlying technology to help with AI training.
In related news, Monster Hunter Wilds' upcoming Switch 2 port, with all its free DLC updates - including new monsters - will be available 4th December. It's set to arrive with local co-op.

item.title: A free next-gen update is coming to Metro 2033 Redux and Metro Last Light Redux on 22nd October for PC (29th October for consoles). Read more
item.description:
A free next-gen update is coming to Metro 2033 Redux and Metro Last Light Redux on 22nd October for PC (29th October for consoles).
The update comes as the Metro series passes 50 million copies sold worldwide, 16 years on from the original Metro 2033's release.
The studio stresses that the update "isn't a full remaster or remake", but "the original Metro Redux experience and aesthetic has been preserved" with the addition of 4K textures across all platforms, improved animations, higher-quality audio, and richer environmental detail, alongside a batch of community-requested bug fixes and quality-of-life changes.
On PlayStation 5, PS5 Pro, and Xbox Series X/S, the update adds native support with platform-specific extras, including PSSR on PS5 Pro, TSR upscaling and anti-aliasing on Xbox Series X, and spatial audio on Xbox platforms more broadly.
Console players will also be able to run the games at native 4K/60fps or upscaled 4K/120fps on compatible displays, with upgraded lighting, shadows and particle effects, DualSense Adaptive Triggers and Xbox Impulse Triggers, hardware tessellation and displacement, and power-saving modes on both platforms.
Xbox players additionally get Play Anywhere and handheld support, while on PC, the update brings DLSS support alongside its own spatial audio and quality-of-life fixes.
Full patch notes are being saved for launch, but the update will be free for all existing owners of Metro 2033 Redux and Metro Last Light Redux on PC via Steam, Epic Games Store, Windows Store, and GOG, and PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.
The update also sets the stage for Metro 2039, which is slated to release on 4th February. Eurogamer went hands-on with the game back in August, with our Dom writing that "making games is hard under normal circumstances, but having played about two hours of Metro 2039 I'm floored by what the team has managed here."
"As well as being a competent shooter with remarkable graphics and a story inspired by the harshest of real world events, the crushing sense of claustrophobia and threat humming in the world of Metro 2039 makes previous games in the series seem almost relaxed. They say diamonds are formed under pressure, I suppose, which I say to Ulmer."

item.title: Micron has warned that global RAM shortages show no sign of easing, telling investors on its earnings call that it has already sold most of next year's production. Read more
item.description:
Micron has warned that global RAM shortages show no sign of easing, telling investors on its earnings call that it has already sold most of next year's production.
As reported by The Register, CEO and chair Sanjay Mehrotra suggested customers should brace for prices well above what they paid in 2026, adding demand would keep outstripping supply through 2027 and into 2028, and calling the industry's supply-demand balance "only getting tighter".
The CEO also admitted that Micron does "not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance".
As most of the capacity is booked for the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) needed for AI datacentres, the big three memory manufacturers - which includes Samsung - have very little dedicated to consumer-grade memory, which caused their prices to shoot up.
That has, in turn, pushed up the prices of pretty much every consumer electronic device that uses these chips, including game consoles like the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2 - all of which have gone up in price several times in some cases. Valve's Steam Machine also launched at a much higher price than Valve expected, and the company hinted it may even have to raise prices again.
The company plans to bring new factories online in 2028, backed by $25 billion in planned capex for the first half of its new financial year, but executives cautioned that the extra capacity won't bring immediate relief on price or availability.
Mehrotra explained that HBM is growing in demand faster than the DRAM used in servers, and said Micron is working to lift its margins on HBM, which currently trails DRAM in profitability.
That said, Micron's cloud memory unit, which covers HBM, posted an 83 per cent gross margin in Q4, up from 59 per cent a year earlier, while its core datacenter business, selling more DRAM, hit 90 per cent, up from 41 per cent. Datacenter SSD sales almost hit $10 billion for the quarter, over 1,000 per cent higher year-on-year.
The company also highlighted its work with Nvidia on NV-HBM, billed as the industry's first custom HBM4E implementation for next-generation GPUs and NVLink Fusion platforms, and said AI-driven demand for context memory storage is widening the market for its NAND-based SSDs.
Samsung, one of the largest manufacturers of memory and storage in the world, also recently delivered bad news for anyone hoping the global component shortages will ease up soon, revealing in an earnings call that it expects the crisis to continue getting worse into next year.

item.description:
Buoyed by some commendatory early reviews and fantastic initial player numbers, Gears of War: E-Day has found a solid audience a weekend before general release. And a large part of its appeal is the combat; I noted in my review I think it's the tightest Gears has ever been, augmented by some innovative thinking around the series' (in)famous weaponry, and a combat system that allows for a gushing release of tension with every wet, crunchy kill.
And it turns out there's a lot more intricate thought behind this eruption of violence than perhaps people realise, as I discovered in an interview with Coalition studio art director Aryan Hanbeck, brand director Nicole Fawcett, and creative director Matt Searcy.
"Think about getting a headshot, right, a really good headshot," says Hanbeck. "A lot of work goes into that moment, into what happens on the screen when you take a headshot. There's an audio component to that, too, as well as all the effects - how high the blood spurts go, how much mist we leave behind, what the body does afterwards… So, it's not just the weapon itself, it's what you see and hear when you do what it's supposed to do, or when you get up close and you melee with [your Lancer or Breechshot] or execute an enemy, which is really cool."
"And there's a big investment in gore in this game," adds Searcy. "That's a huge aspect of [what makes combat so satisfying]."
"We had this feeling that fans were getting a bit desensitised to the violence in Gears, because you're just going around doing all sorts of stuff and blood was a little bit more stylised in the past few games," Hanbeck continues. "So, to make you feel every single kill, we wanted the game to be a bit more realistic - not enough for you to get grossed out, but enough to be like 'wow, some shit's gone down in this world'."
And you know what? It works. Because this Gears of War game is much more centered around humans and the civilian victims as the Locust invaders emerge into the city of Kalona. The violence and bloodshed feel a lot closer to home. It's still very cartoony and probably more akin to something like Tarantino than anything else, but the wetness and crunchyness of its violence hits hard. Searcy told me, when we were chatting about E-Day's difficulty, that every encounter was designed to almost feel like a spring: that there is this coiled build-up and then an energetic release, and that the brutality and violence are a way of realising that moment to moment.
"We've got skeletons inside all the bodies, we've got some fun weapons that expose that a bit later on in the game, we've got crazy dismemberment, blood pooling… a whole bunch of stuff," Hanbeck says, grinning. "It's all there for that same, cathartic reason." When I was previewing the game, I tell the team, my partner entered the room and told me that this was a very 'wet' game. They laugh, and Searcy replies: "To be fair, every time I show my wife a trailer I'm working on, she's like, 'eww' [laughter]. I guess if you don't play Gears all the time, that's a fair first reaction!"
It provokes a conversation about Gears' identity; it's not exactly a satire like Helldivers or Starship Troopers or something, but it doesn't take itself super seriously, either. "It's not a game or franchise where we want to take ourselves so seriously," Fawcett reflects. "And I think it's the contrast that makes Gears so special: it's not one or the other. The humorous moments are usually kind-of relatable like soldier talk, gallows humour, dark humour - and we've been trying to get back to that squad banter that's kind of dark but you can't help but laugh at. Even Marcus… he's this super stoic character that's dry and grunting all the time, and every now and then he'll say something and you'll just [chuckles]. That's Gears: it's not a bleak, apocalyptic story - even though there's a horrible backdrop event happening, and what the characters are going through is absolutely horrific - there is this glimmer of hope, there's levity."
And, in many ways, that's what the violence and blood and gore is doing: it's providing a counterpoint to the high-tension, high-stakes combat that makes up so much of what E-Day is. Pairing moments of levity with grimdark storytelling contrasts well with how you can survive a firefight by the skin of your teeth, by somehow landing your last Longshot round inside a Boomer's skull and watching it coat your teammates in viscera. I praised this well-balanced execution in my review, and a cursory look around the internet will tell you it's landing well with the Gears audience, too. It must be vindicating for The Coalition, even if the mood at the studio is dour for other Xbox-related layoff reasons right now.
You can expect a full review of Gears of War E-Day next week, once I've had time to test out both the Horde and PvP modes. E-Day's first Season kicked off with the Early Access release yesterday and will be live for eight weeks, ending on 1st December. Ranked modes for PvP arrive on 13th October. The game sees a general release on 6th October, with early adopters able to play it right now.

item.description:
Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Bertie's witcher skills are a bit rusty; Dom goes through the Gears; Kelsey enjoys a horror game that feels just like home; and Chris does an incredible impression of a butler that no one acknowledged.
But enough of that: what have you been playing this week?
And don't forget we have an entire dusty archive of previous What We've Been Playings, just in case you don't trust your memory any more and want to check which games you've played and see what you thought of them.
It's weird returning to a game I think I know really well only to discover I don't really know it that well any more at all. The familiarity slowly dribbles back and broad strokes of the game I can of course remember, but that muscle memory that was once so readily there has gone. I bumbled around like an idiot in The Witcher 3 for a couple of hours when revisiting it for the Remastered release this week. I felt like Roach stranded on a rooftop.
I compared the game a lot to The Blood of Dawnwalker while I played, too, which isn't a surprise given how similar they are, and in how they're directed by the same person, Konrad Tomaszkiewicz (and made by many of the same people). And stood side by side, The Witcher 3 holds up remarkably well, which is impressive given that it's now 11 years old.
Indeed, The Witcher 3 even outdoes Dawnwalker in some regards (perhaps many regards). One particular example is the city of Novigrad and its size and interactivity, and the sheer number of people bumbling around, swearing at you. It's a place like few others I've experienced in a role-playing game, and I've said it before and I'll say it again: that's one of gaming's great cities, that is.
Let's see what GTA 6 says when it comes out in November, eh?
I've been reviewing this game for the past week, and it's taken me a much larger chunk of time than I thought it would to grit my teeth and push through the Hardcore difficulty than I thought - there's at least 20 hours of game in the campaign alone if you're playing on any of the more advanced difficulties. I'll be staying on the game to test out Horde and PvP in the coming days (God, I hope my old-person reflexes don't humiliate me too much), and I am not upset about that prospect, either. It's nice to have a game that focuses this much on catharsis and release when the industry is in such dire straits.
I unfortunately haven't had much time or energy to play anything this week that isn't embargoed, but I did make time to watch Jacksepticeye's playthrough of Silent Hill: Townfall with my housemate after playing it myself a few weeks ago and damn, what a game! It also definitely helps that Townfall is where my favourite in-game place - Silent Hill - and my home, the UK, have finally managed to collide. I might be a little biased in that regard, but still, if you like Silent Hill in any shape or form, play it!
It still feels surreal that Konami has not only revived Silent Hill as an IP, but has managed to do it with real style and fervour. Silent Hill 2 Remake has a special place in my heart of course, and Silent Hill f was pretty good - soulslite combat aside - but the publisher has really nailed things with Silent HillL Townfall, and I am so excited to see Screen Burn hopefully get a lot more attention off the back of this.
I managed to achieve the fabled both-parents-go-out-child-free moment for the first time in an age this past weekend, for a nice low-key gathering around a friend's. We were supposed to bring something to play (not a video game, obviously; something a normal person might bring with them to play) as well as a dish, but everybody forgot, so we ended up with a lot of desserts and not a lot to do afterwards for a quick laugh.
Heads Up! became the solution and it was, frankly, better than any new or clever or convoluted game, video or otherwise that I could've dug up to bring around myself. If you're unfamiliar, it's essentially Articlate! (which is basically Pictionary but with talking instead of drawing). Nobody kept score, everyone kept flicking up on the phone to pass and down to mark the answer correct, when it's really the other way round (or is it?! I don't even know myself), and even in these entirely non-competitive circumstances I found it very hard not to get annoyed at someone not immediately recognising my note-perfect impression for the word "Butler". Anyway! Sometimes the classics are the best.
